Reported practices emphasize iterative prompting and content generation, with less consistent use of needs assessment and feedback loops. Institutional barriers including limited policy, training, and infrastructure were widely reported. These findings provide preliminary empirical support for the DOT Framework as a descriptive model of practitioner beliefs and practices, while also highlighting gaps between design-oriented theory and current implementation. The study contributes an initial measurement structure and identifies directions for confirmatory validation and outcome-based research linking AI-supported design practices to instructional quality.

AI.tldr: A cross-sectional survey (n=72) of higher education practitioners reveals favorable views of AI as pedagogical support but strong commitments to human oversight. Factor analysis identified three belief factors (AI Functional Capabilities, Oversight & Governance, Instructor Collaboration & Planning). Practitioners use iterative prompting and content generation but lack needs assessment and feedback loops. Institutional barriers (policy, training, infrastructure) are widespread. The study provides preliminary support for the DOT Framework as a descriptive model.
AI.motivation: To empirically examine higher education practitioners' beliefs, behaviors, and institutional conditions regarding AI integration in teaching and learning, grounded in the DOT Framework (design thinking + open systems theory).
AI.method: Cross-sectional survey (n=72) of higher education practitioners; exploratory factor analysis on 19 belief items identifying a three-factor structure; descriptive analysis of usage patterns, design practices, and institutional barriers.
AI.result: Three-factor structure (α=.90): AI Functional Capabilities, Oversight and Governance, Instructor Collaboration and Planning. Practitioners favor AI for pedagogy but insist on human oversight. Practices focus on iterative prompting/content generation; needs assessment and feedback loops are underused. Widespread institutional barriers (policy, training, infrastructure).
AI.conclusion: Preliminary empirical support for the DOT Framework as a descriptive model; identifies gaps between design-oriented theory and current practice; contributes initial measurement structure; calls for confirmatory validation and outcome-based research linking AI-supported design to instructional quality.

title: VLAConf: Calibrated Task-Success Confidence for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Confidence estimation for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models is essential for robots to perform manipulation tasks in the open world, providing crucial signals for risk-sensitive decision-making and failure anticipation. Existing confidence estimation methods typically rely on ensemble-based paradigms or action-token probabilities to predict the likelihood of task success. However, they still encounter challenges in computational efficiency and cross-architecture generalizability. These methods usually require repeated sampling, leading to inference inefficiency, and are restricted to VLA models with discrete action outputs, making them difficult to apply to continuous action spaces. To address this issue, we propose VLAConf, a one-class discriminative confidence framework. By leveraging frozen pretrained VLA internal representations, VLAConf directly estimates step-wise anomaly scores in a single forward pass using a lightweight confidence head, thereby eliminating the overhead of exhaustive resampling. We additionally use step-conditioned modeling to encode rollout-phase information along the manipulation trajectory. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark demonstrate that VLAConf significantly improves the quality of the confidence signal constructed for post-hoc calibration, outperforming existing baselines by a large margin in inference efficiency. The effectiveness of VLAConf is further validated in real-robot experiments. To access the source code and supplementary videos, visit https://sites.google.com/view/vlaconf.

AI.tldr: VLAConf is a one-class discriminative confidence estimation framework for Vision-Language-Action models that uses frozen internal representations and a lightweight confidence head to compute step-wise anomaly scores efficiently in a single forward pass, outperforming prior methods in both confidence quality and inference efficiency on LIBERO benchmarks and real-robot experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing confidence estimation methods for VLA models suffer from computational inefficiency due to repeated sampling and lack cross-architecture generalizability, being restricted to models with discrete action outputs and unable to handle continuous action spaces.
AI.method: VLAConf leverages frozen pretrained VLA internal representations with a lightweight confidence head to directly estimate step-wise anomaly scores in a single forward pass, using step-conditioned modeling to encode rollout-phase information along the manipulation trajectory.
AI.result: VLAConf significantly improves confidence signal quality for post-hoc calibration on the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming existing baselines by a large margin in inference efficiency, with further validation on real-robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed one-class discriminative framework effectively addresses the efficiency and generalizability limitations of prior confidence estimation methods for VLA models, providing a practical solution for risk-sensitive robot manipulation.

title: Differentiable Belief-based Opponent Shaping
summary: Human coordination often relies on the ability to influence the beliefs of others through strategic action. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, opponent shaping attempts to replicate this influence, though existing methods typically operate within an opponent's parameter, policy, or value space. Meanwhile, belief-manipulation techniques in hidden-role games often rely on hard-coded objectives, such as deception or belief saturation. We propose Differentiable Belief-based Opponent Shaping (D-BOS), a first-order method that treats each observer's belief as the shaped opponent state and differentiates through $k$-step softmax-Bayes belief dynamics. Rather than explicitly rewarding deceptive or cooperative behavior, our method treats the belief state as the target for shaping. This allows the optimal strategy to emerge naturally from the environment's reward structure. This belief-space formulation provides an opponent-shaping signal by differentiating through opponent belief updates, and naturally extends to multiple observers by aggregating gradients over their individual inferred belief trajectories. Empirically, D-BOS outperforms PPO and BBM in hidden-role games, with the largest gains in mixed-motive settings.

AI.tldr: D-BOS is a first-order method that shapes opponents by differentiating through belief dynamics (k-step softmax-Bayes), treating belief states as the target for shaping rather than using hard-coded objectives, and outperforms PPO/BBM in hidden-role games especially in mixed-motive settings.
AI.motivation: Existing opponent shaping methods operate in parameter/policy/value spaces, while belief-manipulation techniques in hidden-role games rely on hard-coded objectives (e.g., deception). There is a need for a principled, differentiable method that allows optimal behavior to emerge naturally from the reward structure.
AI.method: D-BOS treats each observer's belief as the shaped opponent state, differentiates through k-step softmax-Bayes belief dynamics, and aggregates gradients over multiple observers' inferred belief trajectories. It uses first-order gradients rather than explicit reward engineering for deception or cooperation.
AI.result: D-BOS outperforms PPO and BBM in hidden-role games, with the largest performance gains observed in mixed-motive settings.
AI.conclusion: The belief-space formulation for opponent shaping is effective, allowing strategic behavior to emerge from the environment's reward structure without hard-coded social objectives, and naturally extends to multi-observer settings.

title: EXACT-MPPI: Exact Signed-Distance Navigation for Arbitrary-Footprint Robots from Point Clouds via Path Integral Control
summary: Ground robots often carry payloads, implements, or other attachments that turn their effective footprint into complex, non-convex shapes. Navigating safely through clutter then requires reasoning about this true geometry, yet most local planners simplify it with convex or inflated proxies and rasterize sensor data into occupancy grids or distance fields. Both choices eliminate feasible motions when clearance is comparable to the footprint geometry. We present EXACT-MPPI, a training-free local navigation framework that maps local point-cloud observations and sparse guidance directly to motion commands, without any intermediate map representation. The framework embeds an analytic, exact signed-distance evaluator into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller. The footprint is represented as a simple polygon for general convex or concave planar shapes, with a rectangle-cover specialization for faster evaluation of rectilinear footprints, enabling footprint-aware collision costs without convex decomposition, inflation, or learned encoders. During each MPPI rollout, observed obstacle points are transformed into the predicted body frame and evaluated against the footprint. All operations are batched in JAX, leveraging GPU parallelism for real-time receding-horizon control. Experiments show that EXACT-MPPI accelerates batched distance evaluation over a learned point-to-robot baseline, preserves feasible motion where convex-footprint planners fail, and remains robust under dense static and moving obstacles. The same framework deploys on differential-drive, Ackermann, omnidirectional, and hybrid-mode platforms by changing only the footprint description and motion model without per-platform training. Pairing exact footprint geometry with sampling-based predictive control thus offers a practical, training-free path to footprint-aware local navigation across diverse robots.

AI.tldr: EXACT-MPPI is a training-free local navigation framework that uses an exact signed-distance evaluator embedded in an MPPI controller to handle complex, non-convex robot footprints, mapping point-cloud data directly to motion commands without intermediate map representations or convex approximations. It achieves real-time performance via GPU-parallelized JAX batching and works across multiple robot types with only footprint and motion model changes.
AI.motivation: Ground robots often carry attachments that create non-convex footprints; existing local planners simplify this geometry with convex/inflated proxies and rasterize sensor data into grids, eliminating feasible motions when clearance is comparable to footprint geometry.
AI.method: The framework embeds an analytic exact signed-distance evaluator into an MPPI controller. Footprint is represented as a simple polygon (with rectangle-cover specialization for rectilinear shapes). Observed obstacle points are transformed into predicted body frames during rollouts and evaluated against the footprint. All operations are batched in JAX for GPU parallelism.
AI.result: EXACT-MPPI accelerates batched distance evaluation over a learned point-to-robot baseline, preserves feasible motion where convex-footprint planners fail, and remains robust under dense static and moving obstacles. It deploys on differential-drive, Ackermann, omnidirectional, and hybrid-mode platforms without per-platform training.
AI.conclusion: Pairing exact footprint geometry with sampling-based predictive control offers a practical, training-free path to footprint-aware local navigation across diverse robots.

title: Hallucination Mitigation with Agentic AI, Nested Learning, and AI Sustainability via Semantic Caching
summary: Hallucination remains a major reliability barrier for production LLM systems, particularly in multi-agent pipelines where unsupported claims can propagate unchecked across stages. This paper adapts a HOPE-inspired Nested Learning architecture with Continuum Memory Systems (CMS) and semantic similarity caching to a hybrid benchmark of 310 prompts combining 217 epistemic-uncertainty prompts and 93 fabrication-induction stress-test prompts. A three-stage agentic pipeline orchestrated via the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) is evaluated with five KPIs -- FCD (Factual Claim Density), FGR (Factual Grounding References), FDF (Fictional Disclaimer Frequency), ECS (Explicit Contextualization Score), and OSR (Observability Score Ratio) -- aggregated into THS (Total Hallucination Score) across five weighting configurations to study mitigation-observability trade-offs. FDF, ECS, OSR, and FGR are subtracted as mitigation signals, so that a more negative THS indicates stronger mitigation. The FrontEndAgent is configured as a high-stochasticity generator (temperature = 1.0) to produce a realistic hallucination baseline, while the SecondLevelReviewer and ThirdLevelReviewer operate as progressive correctors. This asymmetric design yields end-to-end THS reductions of -31.3% to -35.9% across five weighting configurations. Semantic caching achieves 440 cache hits over 930 potential calls (47.3% hit rate), reducing LLM invocations to 490, lowering energy and CO2e footprint, and making multi-stage review pipelines operationally viable at production scale. ExtremeObservability attains the most negative final THS (-0.0709), confirming that observability-heavy configurations reinforce rather than compromise mitigation. These findings suggest that memory-augmented multi-agent designs can jointly improve factual reliability, operational efficiency, and auditability without model retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts a HOPE-inspired Nested Learning architecture with Continuum Memory Systems and semantic caching to a hybrid benchmark of 310 prompts, evaluated across a three-stage agentic pipeline via the Open Floor Protocol. The approach achieves -31.3% to -35.9% THS reduction, 47.3% semantic cache hit rate, and demonstrates that memory-augmented multi-agent designs improve factual reliability, operational efficiency, and auditability without model retraining.
AI.motivation: Hallucination is a major reliability barrier for production LLM systems, particularly in multi-agent pipelines where unsupported claims can propagate unchecked across stages. The paper aims to mitigate hallucination without requiring model retraining.
AI.method: Adapts a HOPE-inspired Nested Learning architecture with Continuum Memory Systems (CMS) and semantic similarity caching. Evaluates on a hybrid benchmark of 310 prompts (217 epistemic-uncertainty + 93 fabrication-induction stress-test prompts) using a three-stage agentic pipeline orchestrated via Open Floor Protocol (OFP). Asymmetric design: FrontEndAgent (high-stochasticity, temperature=1.0), SecondLevelReviewer and ThirdLevelReviewer (progressive correctors). Five KPIs (FCD, FGR, FDF, ECS, OSR) aggregated into THS across five weighting configurations.
AI.result: End-to-end THS reductions of -31.3% to -35.9% across five weighting configurations. Semantic caching achieved 440 cache hits over 930 potential calls (47.3% hit rate), reducing LLM invocations to 490. ExtremeObservability achieved most negative final THS (-0.0709), confirming observability-heavy configurations reinforce mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Memory-augmented multi-agent designs can jointly improve factual reliability, operational efficiency, and auditability without model retraining. Observability-heavy configurations reinforce rather than compromise hallucination mitigation. Semantic caching makes multi-stage review pipelines operationally viable at production scale by reducing energy and CO2e footprint.

title: FLIP: Real-Time and Resilient Formation Planning for Large-Scale DIstributed Swarms via Point Cloud Registration
summary: Traditional large-scale formation planning either oversimplify the formation representation which leads to poor performance, or they employ complete collaborative relationships, which results in excessive computational load. To achieve high-performance and large-scale formation planning, we transform the Optimal Formation Position Sequence \cite{c1} (OFPS) calculation problem into a spatiotemporal Point Cloud Registration (PCR) problem. Each agent derives its OFPS by distributively computing the matching result between current positions and the desired formation positions of all other agents. Then each agent optimizes the cooperative formation trajectory by using OFPS. We leverage the PCR method with outlier rejection to rapidly perform large-scale formation position registration. This prevents suboptimal trajectories and failed agents from propagating through the cooperative network and affecting more agents. Consequently, we uniformly achieve resilient, efficient, and distributed trajectory planning for large-scale swarms. The effectiveness and the superiority of the proposed method are demonstrated through large-scale simulations of 120-drone formation, and rigorous benchmarking against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.

AI.tldr: A distributed formation planning method for large-scale swarms that reinterprets Optimal Formation Position Sequence (OFPS) as a spatiotemporal Point Cloud Registration (PCR) problem, using outlier rejection to achieve resilient, efficient, and scalable trajectory planning, validated with 120-drone simulations.
AI.motivation: Traditional large-scale formation planning suffers from either oversimplified representations causing poor performance or complete collaborative relationships causing excessive computational load.
AI.method: Transform OFPS calculation into a spatiotemporal Point Cloud Registration (PCR) problem; each agent computes its OFPS distributively by matching current positions with desired formation positions of all agents; uses PCR with outlier rejection for robust large-scale position registration.
AI.result: Demonstrated effectiveness and superiority through large-scale 120-drone formation simulations and rigorous benchmarking against SOTA methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method uniformly achieves resilient, efficient, and distributed trajectory planning for large-scale swarms, preventing suboptimal trajectories and failed agents from propagating through the cooperative network.

title: Robust and Efficient Guardrails with Latent Reasoning
summary: Maintaining the safety of large language models (LLMs) is crucial as they are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. Existing safety guardrails typically rely on single-pass classification or, more recently, distilled reasoning. Reasoning-based guardrails significantly outperform classification-only baselines, but they incur substantial query latency and token overhead that make them impractical for highthroughput deployment. To address this challenge, we propose COLAGUARD, a guardrail model that transfers multi-step safety reasoning into a continuous latent space through a stage-wise training curriculum, enabling direct hidden-state propagation at inference. Evaluated on ten prompt- and response-moderation settings spanning eight safety benchmarks, COLAGUARD improves macro-F1 by 8.24 points over Llama Guard 3 and matches our explicit reasoning baseline, GuardReasoner, in macroF1 while delivering a 12.9X speedup and 22.4X reduction in token usage. Our results suggest that latent reasoning offers a practical alternative to explicit rationale generation for deployable guardrails, jointly improving safety robustness and inference efficiency rather than treating them as competing objectives.

AI.tldr: COLAGUARD transfers multi-step safety reasoning into continuous latent space via stage-wise training, achieving 12.9X speedup and 22.4X token reduction over explicit reasoning guardrails while matching or exceeding their accuracy across 8 safety benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning-based guardrails (e.g., GuardReasoner) outperform classification-only baselines but incur impractical latency and token overhead for high-throughput deployment. The paper aims to bridge the gap between safety reasoning quality and inference efficiency.
AI.method: Proposes COLAGUARD, which transfers multi-step safety reasoning into continuous latent space through a stage-wise training curriculum, enabling direct hidden-state propagation at inference without explicit rationale generation.
AI.result: Improves macro-F1 by 8.24 points over Llama Guard 3; matches GuardReasoner in macro-F1 while delivering 12.9X speedup and 22.4X reduction in token usage across 10 prompt- and response-moderation settings spanning 8 safety benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Latent reasoning offers a practical alternative to explicit rationale generation for deployable guardrails, jointly improving safety robustness and inference efficiency rather than treating them as competing objectives.

title: PhAIL: A Real-Robot VLA Benchmark and Distributional Methodology
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables. Dataset, analysis pipeline, and paper source: https://phail.ai and https://github.com/Positronic-Robotics/phail-paper
summary: Real-world evaluation of vision-language-action (VLA) policies still rests on binary success rate at a fixed timeout with $N \le 25$ rollouts per condition, almost always without confidence intervals or paired statistical comparison; these cohort sizes struggle to resolve close comparisons reliably. We introduce PhAIL (Physical AI Leaderboard, https://phail.ai), an open real-robot benchmark on a Franka FR3 (dataset, per-rollout artifacts, and end-to-end reference implementation) of a distributional evaluation methodology: the time-to-success cumulative distribution function (CDF) as the evaluation primitive, with two separated jobs. The first is scoring via Human-Relative Throughput (HRT), a dimensionless scalar with bootstrap confidence intervals, anchored to same-fixture human teleoperation. The second is a significance test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, computed per-object and macro-averaged across objects). On four publicly-available VLAs, the macro-averaged KS test resolves two close comparisons (GR00T vs. ACT, OpenPI vs. ACT) at $N \le 30$ rollouts per (model, object) cell where binary-threshold metrics do not; the closest pair (OpenPI vs. GR00T) remains unresolved within our budget. The best evaluated VLA is $\sim 7\times$ slower per operation (RMST ratio) than the human reference.

AI.tldr: PhAIL introduces a distributional evaluation methodology using time-to-success CDFs, Human-Relative Throughput (HRT) with bootstrap confidence intervals, and KS significance testing, demonstrating improved statistical resolution over binary success rates for VLA policy comparison.
AI.motivation: Current VLA policy evaluation relies on binary success rate with small cohort sizes (N ≤ 25) and lacks confidence intervals or paired statistical comparisons, making it difficult to resolve close performance comparisons reliably.
AI.method: Proposes PhAIL benchmark using time-to-success CDF as evaluation primitive, HRT scalar metric with bootstrap confidence intervals anchored to human teleoperation, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov significance test macro-averaged across objects.
AI.result: On four VLA policies, macro-averaged KS test resolves two close comparisons (GR00T vs. ACT, OpenPI vs. ACT) at N ≤ 30 where binary metrics fail; the closest pair (OpenPI vs. GR00T) remains unresolved. Best VLA is ~7× slower per operation than human reference.
AI.conclusion: Distributional evaluation with time-to-success CDFs and KS testing provides better statistical resolution for VLA policy comparison than binary success rate metrics, though some close comparisons still require larger budgets.

title: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap in Reinforcement Learning-Based Industrial Dispatching through Execution Semantics
comment: Accepted for publication at the 24th IEEE International Conference on Industrial Informatics (INDIN 2026), held from 26 to 29 July 2026 in Melbourne, Australia
summary:
Event-driven scheduling policies are increasingly deployed in industrial environments, where decisions are made under asynchronous and partially observed system states. As a result, decision states are not temporally consistent, action admissibility is not explicitly defined, and the origin of execution errors remains ambiguous. These issues limit both reliability and interpretability.
  To address this gap, a policy-neutral execution and measurement layer is proposed to mediate between scheduling policies and the industrial execution environment. The layer constructs decision-valid snapshots from asynchronous event streams, defines a standardized execution contract with explicit action admissibility, and records outcomes as divergences between policy intent, transactional outcomes, physical execution, and human intervention. This enables a separation between decision semantics and execution behavior and makes deployment mismatch observable and structurally attributable.
  The proposed framework is evaluated using a discrete-event simulation. The results show analytical benefits across all observation lag regimes, as undifferentiated execution failures are transformed into structured, typed outcomes with full attribution coverage. Operational benefits are strongest under low observation lag, where avoidable execution errors can be prevented before commitment. Overall, the layer turns execution uncertainty into supervisory data for evaluation and policy refinement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a policy-neutral execution and measurement layer that mediates between scheduling policies and industrial environments, converting asynchronous event streams into decision-valid snapshots, standardizing action admissibility, and attributing execution divergences. The framework improves reliability and interpretability by making deployment mismatches observable.
AI.motivation: Event-driven scheduling policies face issues with temporally inconsistent decision states, undefined action admissibility, and ambiguous execution errors, which limit reliability and interpretability in industrial environments.
AI.method: A policy-neutral execution and measurement layer is designed to: (1) construct decision-valid snapshots from asynchronous event streams, (2) define a standardized execution contract with explicit action admissibility, (3) record outcome divergences across policy intent, transactional outcomes, physical execution, and human intervention.
AI.result: Evaluated via discrete-event simulation; undifferentiated execution failures become structured, typed outcomes with full attribution coverage across all observation lag regimes. Operational benefits are strongest under low observation lag, preventing avoidable execution errors before commitment.
AI.conclusion: The layer transforms execution uncertainty into supervisory data for evaluation and policy refinement, enabling separation between decision semantics and execution behavior with structural attribution of deployment mismatches.

title: MARS Policy: Multimodality Only When It Matters
summary: Imitation learning has become a cornerstone for solving complex robotic manipulation tasks. In particular, multimodality, which enables robots to capture diverse yet valid behavioral patterns, has driven the rapid emergence of generative policies as a dominant paradigm in robot learning. However, achieving such multimodality typically relies on stochastic noise initialization and iterative denoising procedures, resulting in substantial training complexity and low inference efficiency. Meanwhile, not all phases of a robotic task inherently require behavioral diversity. Motivated by this insight, we propose the Modality-Adaptive Robot Sampling (MARS) policy, which adaptively invokes tailored stochasticity only when it is truly beneficial, while reverting to an efficient deterministic learning during single-modal phases. In other words, the proper amount of noise is injected only at the proper time. By selectively activating multimodal generation, MARS policy bridges the gap between the multimodal capability of generative policies and the superior training and inference efficiency of deterministic models. Empirical studies across 8 simulated and 4 real-world tasks demonstrate that MARS exhibits robust multimodal expressivity and high efficiency, with a 16.67% success rate improvement and an 83.20% inference latency reduction in real-world tests. Counterintuitively, MARS also outpaces deterministic policies in training efficiency on near-deterministic tasks by more effectively modeling nuanced action diversity.

AI.tldr: MARS policy adaptively switches between deterministic learning (for single-modal phases) and stochastic generation (for multimodal phases) in robotic imitation learning, achieving 16.67% higher success rate and 83.20% lower inference latency compared to prior generative policies.
AI.motivation: Current generative policies for robotic manipulation rely on stochastic noise and iterative denoising for multimodality, which incurs high training complexity and low inference efficiency, even though not all task phases require behavioral diversity.
AI.method: MARS adaptively activates multimodal generation (noise injection) only when beneficial, and falls back to efficient deterministic learning during single-modal phases, bridging generative and deterministic policy paradigms.
AI.result: Evaluated on 8 simulated and 4 real-world tasks; achieves 16.67% success rate improvement and 83.20% inference latency reduction in real-world tests; also outperforms deterministic policies in training efficiency on near-deterministic tasks.
AI.conclusion: Selective stochasticity (modality-adaptive sampling) effectively balances multimodal expressivity with training/inference efficiency, challenging the necessity of full-time noise-driven generation in robot imitation learning.

title: The Importance of Out-of-Band Metadata for Safe Autonomous Agents: The Redpanda Agentic Data Plane
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Published at SAO '26 (co-located with ACM CAIS '26)
summary:
AI agents are increasingly expected to operate as digital employees: accessing enterprise data, making decisions, and taking actions autonomously. But agents are simultaneously less predictable than humans -- prone to hallucination, misinterpretation, and adversarial manipulation -- and more technically capable: with deep system knowledge and high-throughput interfaces cascading damage at machine speed. This combination makes it unsafe to rely on agents to faithfully interpret or propagate security-critical metadata such as access policies, data classifications, and behavioral constraints.
  We present the Redpanda Agentic Data Plane (ADP), an architecture built around out-of-band metadata channels: infrastructure pathways that carry security context, policy signals, and audit trails deterministically, entirely outside the agent's read and write path and across heterogeneous infrastructure. These channels enforce governance at every stage of the agent lifecycle -- scoping data access on the way in, constraining actions during execution, and capturing tamper-proof transcripts on the way out.
  We demonstrate ADP with a multi-agent portfolio rebalancing system in which autonomous agents monitor markets, make trade decisions, and execute orders across isolated client accounts -- with per-client data scoping, trade approval thresholds, and tamper-proof audit trails all enforced by out-of-band channels the agents can neither see nor bypass.

AI.tldr: The Redpanda Agentic Data Plane (ADP) uses out-of-band metadata channels to enforce security governance for AI agents operating as digital employees, carrying policy signals, data scoping, and audit trails entirely outside the agent's read/write path.
AI.motivation: AI agents are unsafe for enterprise use because they combine unpredictability (hallucination, misinterpretation, adversarial manipulation) with high technical capability (deep system access, high-throughput interfaces), making it unreliable to trust agents with security-critical metadata like access policies and data classifications.
AI.method: Out-of-band metadata channels: infrastructure pathways that carry security context, policy signals, and audit trails deterministically outside the agent's read and write path, enforcing governance across the entire agent lifecycle (scoping data access on input, constraining actions during execution, capturing tamper-proof transcripts on output).
AI.result: Demonstrated with a multi-agent portfolio rebalancing system where autonomous agents monitor markets, make trades, and execute orders across isolated client accounts, with per-client data scoping, trade approval thresholds, and tamper-proof audit trails enforced by out-of-band channels that agents cannot see or bypass.
AI.conclusion: ADP provides a viable architecture for deploying AI agents as digital employees by decoupling security enforcement from agent trustworthiness, using infrastructure-level out-of-band channels to govern agent behavior regardless of whether agents are compromised or acting in error.

title: Joint Angle Estimation with Customized Wristband Based on Online Incremental Learning
summary: Intelligent wearable technology plays an increasingly important role in human-computer interaction, motion, and health monitoring. To ensure comfort and practicality of use, one common form for motion monitoring is to utilize soft wearable sensors. However, many research applications regarding wearable sensors are simplistic and difficult to adapt to different situations. This study proposes a system for estimating the angle of the wrist joint using a customized wristband based on an online incremental learning approach. It is a two-stage estimation method: the first stage updates the model based on the wearer's wrist movement characteristics using online learning, integrating real-time data from an IMU as ground truth. The second stage utilizes the updated model for estimation of wrist joint angle solely with the wristband. In other words, model training is completed during data acquisition, allowing the trained model to be used for subsequent angle estimation. This method offers advantages in adapting to data drift caused by variations in different testing configurations, such as the left and right wrists of the same subject, deviations in the wearing position on the same wrist, and even differences among various subjects. The results indicate that the sensors exhibit good performance under strain variations, and the wrist joint trajectory estimation of the proposed system has an approximate error of 15 degree in different scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an online incremental learning system using a soft wristband with IMU-based ground truth to estimate wrist joint angles in two stages: model training during data acquisition followed by angle estimation, achieving ~15° error across different wearing conditions, subjects, and left/right wrists.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of existing soft wearable sensors in motion monitoring, which are often too simplistic and not adaptable to different configurations, by developing a system that can handle data drift caused by variations in wearing position, left/right wrists, and subject differences.
AI.method: A two-stage online incremental learning approach: (1) model updating during data acquisition using real-time IMU data as ground truth, adapting to the wearer's wrist movement characteristics; (2) estimation of wrist joint angle using only the customized wristband without external IMU references.
AI.result: The sensors demonstrate good performance under strain variations, and the wrist joint trajectory estimation achieves an approximate error of 15 degrees across different scenarios (left/right wrists, wearing positions, and between subjects).
AI.conclusion: The online incremental learning system effectively adapts to data drift from various testing configurations, making soft wearable sensors more practical and adaptable for real-world wrist joint angle estimation.

title: LLM-Guided Future Hypotheses for Horizon-Aware Exploration in Multi-Step Robot Manipulation
summary: Multi-step robot manipulation requires acting under uncertainty about how the scene will evolve, making exploration and policy adaptation challenging. We study whether short-horizon, task-consistent future videos can provide useful structured priors for control and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. We formalize this idea through Future-Experience Conditioning (FEC), a simple interface that conditions closed-loop policies on a latent representation of a short future video. In our simulation setup, future clips are generated in three stages, an LLM reasoner operating over a task ontology initialized from the current scene state, a robot-free digital-twin rollout of the intended object motion, and a mask-free video diffusion model that synthesizes a robot-consistent future clip without requiring segmentation at inference. We instantiate this future-conditioning interface primarily with BC and BC+RL, and compare against a future-conditioned Streaming Flow Policy (SFP) baseline on RoboCasa and CALVIN under NoFuture, GTFuture, GenFuture, and WrongFuture. Generated futures improve performance over no-future conditioning, while mismatched futures degrade it, and our BC+RL instantiation achieves the strongest overall results. An average BC+RL learning-curve analysis across 8 CALVIN tasks further shows that GTFuture improves fastest, GenFuture improves earlier and to a higher level than NoFuture, and WrongFuture remains at zero throughout training. These results suggest that short-horizon future videos can serve as useful structured priors for exploration and policy adaptation under imperfect future predictions. https://enact2026.github.io/

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Future-Experience Conditioning (FEC), a method that conditions closed-loop robot policies on latent representations of short future videos to provide structured priors for exploration and policy adaptation. Using a three-stage pipeline (LLM reasoning, digital-twin rollout, video diffusion), FEC is evaluated with BC and BC+RL on RoboCasa and CALVIN, showing that generated futures improve performance over no-future conditioning while mismatched futures degrade it, with BC+RL achieving strongest results.
AI.motivation: Multi-step robot manipulation involves uncertainty about scene evolution, making exploration and policy adaptation challenging. The authors aim to study whether short-horizon, task-consistent future videos can serve as useful structured priors for control and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.
AI.method: FEC conditions closed-loop policies on a latent representation of a short future video. Future clips are generated in three stages: (1) an LLM reasoner operating over a task ontology initialized from the current scene state, (2) a robot-free digital-twin rollout of intended object motion, and (3) a mask-free video diffusion model that synthesizes robot-consistent future clips without requiring inference-time segmentation. The interface is instantiated with BC and BC+RL, compared against a future-conditioned Streaming Flow Policy (SFP) baseline on RoboCasa and CALVIN under NoFuture, GTFuture, GenFuture, and WrongFuture conditions.
AI.result: Generated futures improve performance over no-future conditioning, mismatched futures degrade it, and BC+RL achieves the strongest overall results. Average learning-curve analysis across 8 CALVIN tasks shows GTFuture improves fastest, GenFuture improves earlier and to a higher level than NoFuture, and WrongFuture remains at zero throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Short-horizon future videos can serve as useful structured priors for exploration and policy adaptation under imperfect future predictions.

title: Trends in AI and Human-AI Interaction in Clinical Trials -- A Hybrid Human-AI Exploration
comment: 8 pages plus 2 pages references and appendix
summary: This paper examines records retrieved from the ClinicalTrials.gov registry to characterize temporal trends in AI terminology and the geographical distribution of AI trials. The work also reports on an exploratory hybrid human-AI approach to analyzing human-AI interaction trends in registered clinical trials. The hybrid workflow comprised a frontier generative AI model (GPT-5.5) and human review to screen and categorize records returned by an AI-focused search. The findings indicate a marked increase in AI-related trials over time, with recent growth in references to machine learning, deep learning, chatbots, GPTs, and large language models. Geographically, China and the United States accounted for the largest numbers of AI-related trials, with notable recent increases in several other countries including Italy, France, Spain, the UK and Turkey (Türkiye). In a random sample of 100 records, human and AI classifiers showed good agreement in identifying studies not substantively using AI, but lower agreement in classifying human-AI interaction, particularly where health professional interaction was ambiguous or insufficiently described. Overall, the results suggest that hybrid human-AI screening of clinical trial records is potentially viable, but clearer trial reporting and more precise interaction definitions will benefit the process.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes temporal and geographical trends in AI-related clinical trials using ClinicalTrials.gov data, and evaluates a hybrid human-GPT-5.5 screening approach for classifying human-AI interaction in trial records.
AI.motivation: To characterize the growth and distribution of AI terminology in clinical trials over time and across countries, and to explore the viability of a hybrid human-AI workflow for screening and categorizing AI-related trial records.
AI.method: Records were retrieved from ClinicalTrials.gov. A hybrid workflow combining GPT-5.5 (frontier generative AI) and human review was used to screen and categorize records returned by an AI-focused search. Inter-rater agreement between human and AI classifiers was assessed on a random sample of 100 records.
AI.result: AI-related trials increased markedly over time, with recent growth in references to ML, deep learning, chatbots, GPTs, and LLMs. China and the US had the most AI trials, with increases in Italy, France, Spain, the UK, and Turkey. Human-AI agreement was high for identifying non-substantive AI use but lower for classifying human-AI interaction, especially with ambiguous health professional involvement.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid human-AI screening of clinical trial records is potentially viable, but success depends on clearer trial reporting and more precise definitions of human-AI interaction.

title: Fisher-Preserving Guidance: Training-Free Manifold Constraints for Safe Diffusion Control
summary: Diffusion models are effective for waypoint prediction in visual navigation, but standard sampling and test time guidance can produce unreliable or inefficient trajectories when updates drift off the training manifold. We propose Fisher Preserving Guidance with Outer Product Span Projection, a training-free inference method that avoids large Fisher drift associated with off-distribution actions while optimizing a task objective. Our method computes the Fisher-preserving update via a low-rank Jacobian factorization, requiring only a single backward pass per step and enabling real-time use. We further introduce Truncated Fisher Denoising Sensitivity as an uncertainty signal and use it for robust multi-sample action blending. Experiments on toy and realistic navigation benchmarks, including Maze2D with TSDF-based guidance, PushT with official Diffusion Policy weights, and visual navigation in simulation and on real robots, demonstrate consistent improvements in performance over strong diffusion-policy baselines without additional training.

AI.tldr: Proposes Fisher Preserving Guidance with Outer Product Span Projection, a training-free inference method that prevents off-distribution drift in diffusion-based visual navigation by using low-rank Jacobian factorization and Truncated Fisher Denoising Sensitivity for uncertainty-guided action blending.
AI.motivation: Standard sampling and test-time guidance in diffusion models for waypoint prediction can produce unreliable or inefficient trajectories when updates drift off the training manifold, motivating a method to constrain updates to be Fisher-preserving.
AI.method: Fisher Preserving Guidance with Outer Product Span Projection: a low-rank Jacobian factorization that computes Fisher-preserving updates via a single backward pass per step, plus Truncated Fisher Denoising Sensitivity for robust multi-sample action blending.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong diffusion-policy baselines on Maze2D (with TSDF guidance), PushT (with official Diffusion Policy weights), and visual navigation in both simulation and real robots, without additional training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free inference method effectively avoids off-distribution drift while optimizing task objectives, leading to more reliable and efficient trajectories in visual navigation tasks.

title: Beyond Consensus: Trace-Level Synthesis in Mixture of Agents
summary: When multiple LLM agents solve the same problem, standard practice compresses each agent's reasoning into a majority vote or layered synthesis, treating agreement as the finish line. We show this is unnecessarily lossy: an LLM aggregator that reads complete reasoning traces recovers correct solutions even when agents unanimously agree, with beneficial corrections consistently outweighing harmful ones -- the \emph{aggregation paradox}. Majority voting has a ceiling that perturbation diversity does not raise (error correlations are identical); the aggregator's gain comes from trace-level complementarity, assembling correct intermediate steps from minority chains that voting discards. These findings motivate Self-Consistent Mixture of Agents which generates trace diversity through semantic-preserving input perturbations, safeguards the majority via anchored refinement with provable non-degradation guarantees, and always synthesizes -- never gates on consensus. A single model with perturbation-induced trace variation outperforms heterogeneous model pools across structured reasoning, PhD-level science, competition mathematics, and competitive programming. The unit of aggregation should be the reasoning trace, not the answer.

AI.tldr: LLM aggregators that read full reasoning traces outperform answer-level majority voting because they exploit trace-level complementarity, even when agents unanimously agree. Self-Consistent Mixture of Agents (SC-MoA) uses semantic-preserving perturbations and anchored refinement to achieve this without heterogeneous models.
AI.motivation: Standard practice compresses multi-agent reasoning into majority voting or layered synthesis, which treats agreement as the finish line and discards useful intermediate information. The authors show this is unnecessarily lossy and that trace-level information can recover correct solutions even when agents unanimously agree.
AI.method: Self-Consistent Mixture of Agents (SC-MoA): generates trace diversity via semantic-preserving input perturbations, safeguards majority via anchored refinement with provable non-degradation guarantees, and always synthesizes traces rather than gating on consensus.
AI.result: An LLM aggregator reading complete reasoning traces recovers correct solutions even under unanimous agreement, with beneficial corrections outweighing harmful ones (aggregation paradox). A single model with perturbation-induced trace variation outperforms heterogeneous model pools across structured reasoning, PhD-level science, competition math, and competitive programming.
AI.conclusion: The unit of aggregation should be the reasoning trace, not the answer. Trace-level complementarity from minority chains provides information that answer-level voting discards, and this approach yields stronger performance than using diverse model pools.

title: Replicable Simulation-Based Robot Validation through Provenance
summary: Robot behavior is often validated through simulation-based testing, yet the replicability of such campaigns depends critically on transparent documentation of how tests are configured, executed, and post-processed. We argue that data provenance, coupled with the FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability), addresses this gap by explicitly tracking links between artifacts and by attaching machine-readable metadata about file origins and key design decisions. Moreover, provenance and metadata cannot be treated as an afterthought confined to final datasets; they must be integrated into the testing processes that generate those datasets so that evidence can be reconstructed end-to-end. We demonstrate this by augmenting an existing simulation-based testing framework with provenance tracking and metadata collection mechanisms, and by using these extensions to enrich a mobile robot navigation dataset with structured provenance and FAIR-aligned metadata. Finally, we discuss obstacles encountered in this integration -- such as vocabulary alignment, attribute selection, and adoption of domain standards -- and provide actionable recommendations for implementing provenance-centric, FAIR metadata in robotics validation workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating data provenance and FAIR metadata into simulation-based robot testing to improve replicability, demonstrates it on a mobile robot navigation dataset, and provides recommendations for adoption.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based robot testing lacks replicability due to poor documentation of test configuration, execution, and post-processing. Provenance and FAIR principles can address this gap by linking artifacts and metadata.
AI.method: The authors augment an existing simulation-based testing framework with provenance tracking and metadata collection, then apply it to a mobile robot navigation dataset, adding structured provenance and FAIR-aligned metadata.
AI.result: A demonstration of enriched robot navigation dataset with end-to-end provenance tracking; identification of obstacles including vocabulary alignment, attribute selection, and domain standard adoption.
AI.conclusion: Provenance and metadata must be integrated throughout the testing lifecycle (not as an afterthought). The authors provide actionable recommendations for implementing FAIR metadata in robotics validation workflows.

title: PRO-CUA: Process-Reward Optimization for Computer Use Agents
summary: Computer use agents (CUAs) have shown strong potential for automating complex digital workflows, yet their training remains constrained by costly live environment interaction and limited high-quality supervision. Existing filtered behavior cloning pipelines suffer from imitation bottlenecks, including distribution shift from the expert demonstration and the absence of negative learning signals. Meanwhile, standard trajectory-level reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards, ambiguous credit assignment, and high infrastructure costs for long-horizon GUI interaction. In this work, we propose PRO-CUA, a process-reward optimization framework for training CUAs with iterative step-level reinforcement learning. PRO-CUA decouples on-policy environment interaction from policy optimization: the current policy collects states through live rollouts, generates diverse candidate actions for each state, receives step-level feedback from a process reward model (PRM), and is optimized with group-relative advantages. This design enables dense and flexible credit assignment without relying on golden answers or offline expert trajectories, while reducing distribution shift by training on the agent's own execution states. Experiments on live web benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRO-CUA and the reliability of PRM-guided step-level training.

AI.tldr: PRO-CUA introduces a process-reward optimization framework for training computer use agents via iterative step-level reinforcement learning, using a process reward model to provide dense feedback without relying on expert demonstrations or golden answers.
AI.motivation: Existing CUAs suffer from imitation bottlenecks (distribution shift, lack of negative signals) in behavior cloning, and sparse rewards, ambiguous credit assignment, and high infrastructure costs in trajectory-level RL for long-horizon GUI tasks.
AI.method: PRO-CUA decouples on-policy environment interaction from policy optimization: the current policy collects states via live rollouts, generates diverse candidate actions per state, receives step-level feedback from a process reward model (PRM), and is optimized with group-relative advantages.
AI.result: Experiments on live web benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRO-CUA and the reliability of PRM-guided step-level training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables dense and flexible credit assignment without golden answers or offline expert trajectories, while reducing distribution shift by training on the agent's own execution states.

title: Sample-Efficient Diffusion-based Reinforcement Learning with Critic Guidance
summary: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have achieved great successes by leveraging the multimodality and exploration capability of diffusion policies. Among these approaches, one representative branch focuses on the sampling-based policy optimization. This design enables better exploration capability of the diffusion model, particularly at the beginning of training, but suffer from low exploitation in Q-value information, resulting in a slow policy convergence. Another branch pays attention to gradient-based policy optimization, which sufficiently exploits the gradient of the Q function yet tends to collapse into a unimodal policy with low diversity. To address this issue, we propose CGPO, \textbf{C}ritic-\textbf{G}uided diffusion \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization, which effectively balances exploration and exploitation with the training-free guidance technique integrated into the denoising process of diffusion policy. Concretely, CGPO steers action generation toward high-value regions defined by the critic network and uses the guided actions as regression objectives. In this manner, CGPO reduces the time required to obtain high-quality actions and improves final performance with better balance between the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. We validate the effectiveness of CGPO on 5 MuJoCo locomotion tasks, and CGPO achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with existing diffusion-based RL methods. Notably, CGPO is the first success to incorporate diffusion policy into real-world RL, with its superior performance on Franka robot arm grasping tasks. Our official page is released at https://dingsht.tech/cgpo-webpage.

AI.tldr: CGPO is a critic-guided diffusion policy optimization method that balances exploration and exploitation by integrating training-free guidance into the denoising process of diffusion policies, achieving SOTA on MuJoCo locomotion tasks and the first successful deployment of diffusion policy in real-world RL on Franka robot arm grasping.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based RL methods fall into two branches: sampling-based policy optimization (good exploration but slow convergence due to low exploitation of Q-value information) and gradient-based policy optimization (good exploitation but collapses into unimodal low-diversity policies). CGPO aims to balance exploration and exploitation.
AI.method: CGPO integrates a training-free guidance technique into the denoising process of diffusion policy, steering action generation toward high-value regions defined by the critic network and using these guided actions as regression objectives.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on 5 MuJoCo locomotion tasks compared to existing diffusion-based RL methods, and is the first to successfully incorporate diffusion policy into real-world RL with superior performance on Franka robot arm grasping tasks.
AI.conclusion: CGPO effectively balances exploration-exploitation tradeoff, reduces time to obtain high-quality actions, and improves final performance. It demonstrates the first successful real-world deployment of diffusion policies in RL.

title: The Confidence Shortcut: A Reasoning Failure Mode of Masked Diffusion Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDMs) uniquely support any-order generation, with confidence-based decoding currently serving as the de facto standard inference policy. To optimize for this, recent training schemes attempt to align training mask patterns directly with those observed during generation. However, we argue that confidence-based decoding is inherently misaligned with the logical-flow trajectories required for complex reasoning, and that confidence-aligned training actively entrenches this misalignment. We make this concrete using multi-digit addition, where the decoding strategy prematurely predicts locally easy digits before resolving their long-range dependencies, producing high-confidence errors on challenging inputs. While traditional random masking keeps the failure rate low on this challenging tail, confidence-aligned training amplifies the error rate by an order of magnitude. Across five distinct reasoning tasks, this same pattern emerges with task-dependent severity: confidence-based decoding induces failures on highly complex inputs, and confidence-aligned training exacerbates them. In contrast, random masking -- despite its perceived inefficiency -- robustly preserves the reasoning-trajectory conditionals essential for solving the challenging tail.

AI.tldr: Masked diffusion language models using confidence-based decoding produce high-confidence errors on challenging reasoning tasks, especially when trained with confidence-aligned masking; random masking better preserves reasoning-trajectory conditionals for complex inputs.
AI.motivation: Current masked diffusion language models rely on confidence-based decoding as the standard inference policy, but the authors suspect this approach is fundamentally misaligned with the logical-step-by-step trajectories required for complex reasoning tasks.
AI.method: The authors analyze multi-digit addition and four other reasoning tasks, comparing confidence-based decoding vs. random masking under both standard training and confidence-aligned training schemes. They track error rates and failure patterns on challenging inputs.
AI.result: Confidence-based decoding produces high-confidence errors by prematurely predicting locally easy digits before resolving long-range dependencies. Confidence-aligned training amplifies error rates by an order of magnitude on challenging inputs. Random masking keeps failure rates low and preserves reasoning-trajectory conditionals.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-based decoding is misaligned with complex reasoning; random masking, despite perceived inefficiency, is more robust for challenging reasoning tasks. Confidence-aligned training actively exacerbates this misalignment.

title: BORA: Bridging Offline Reinforcement Learning and Online Residual Adaptation for Real-World Dexterous VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for grounding visual-language understanding into real-world robotic manipulation. However, dexterous manipulation remains challenging for VLA policies due to high-dimensional hand control and compounding execution errors, which makes real-world RL post-training essential for bridging the gap between visually grounded action generation and physically reliable dexterous execution. However, high-dimensional dexterous exploration often triggers temporal inconsistency, sample inefficiency and hardware risks in the real world. To address these challenges, we propose BORA, an offline-to-online RL post-training framework designed for real-world dexterous VLA models. In the offline phase, BORA constructs a critic that takes both the VLM's cognition tokens and action chunks as inputs. This design enables action-conditioned value guidance, allowing the critic to evaluate dexterous hand motions beyond visual context alone. During the subsequent online phase, BORA freezes the VLA base and introduces a lightweight, Human-in-the-Loop (HiL) chunk-wise residual adaptation mechanism to mitigate real-world execution errors and further correct the offline-learned intents within the actual physical environment. By inheriting the offline critic and employing intervention-driven rewards, BORA effectively corrects execution discrepancies and adapts to real-world physical variances while preserving the pretrained policy as a stable prior. Extensive evaluations across five complex real-world dexterous tasks demonstrate that BORA significantly outperforms pure imitation learning and traditional decoupled RL baselines, achieving a 33% absolute increase in average success rate under standard settings and up to a 43% improvement in unseen object generalization.

AI.tldr: BORA is an offline-to-online RL post-training framework for real-world dexterous VLA models that uses a VLM-cognition-aware critic and a lightweight Human-in-the-Loop chunk-wise residual adaptation mechanism to correct execution errors, achieving 33% higher average success rate and 43% improvement in unseen object generalization across five complex dexterous tasks.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation remains challenging for VLA policies due to high-dimensional hand control and compounding execution errors, requiring real-world RL post-training. However, high-dimensional dexterous exploration causes temporal inconsistency, sample inefficiency, and hardware risks in the real world.
AI.method: BORA has two phases: (1) Offline phase - constructs a critic taking both VLM cognition tokens and action chunks as inputs for action-conditioned value guidance; (2) Online phase - freezes the VLA base, introduces a lightweight Human-in-the-Loop (HiL) chunk-wise residual adaptation mechanism, inherits the offline critic, and employs intervention-driven rewards to correct execution discrepancies.
AI.result: Across five complex real-world dexterous tasks, BORA outperforms pure imitation learning and traditional decoupled RL baselines with 33% absolute increase in average success rate under standard settings and up to 43% improvement in unseen object generalization.
AI.conclusion: BORA effectively bridges the gap between visually grounded action generation and physically reliable dexterous execution by correcting execution discrepancies and adapting to real-world physical variances while preserving the pretrained policy as a stable prior.

title: Governing Technical Debt in Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored as production infrastructure: they reason over multiple steps, call tools, act through workflows, and adapt through memory and feedback. These systems create governance challenges that are not fully captured by traditional software or predictive ML technical debt. We define Agentic Technical Debt as the accumulated liability created when prompts, memory, tool schemas, orchestration graphs, control policies, and observability routines are patched together faster than they can be validated, standardized, and governed. We define Stochastic Tax as the recurring operating burden of keeping probabilistic agent behavior within acceptable bounds. The distinction matters: debt is a stock of design and governance liability, while the tax is a flow of operating cost that arises because stochastic agents act through tools and workflows. We outline how managers can make both visible through lightweight dashboards and governance controls.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two key concepts—Agentic Technical Debt (accumulated governance liability from poorly structured agent systems) and Stochastic Tax (ongoing operational costs of managing probabilistic agent behavior)—and proposes lightweight dashboards and governance controls to make both visible to managers.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks for technical debt from traditional software and predictive ML fail to capture the unique governance challenges of agentic AI systems that reason, use tools, adapt through memory, and operate via workflows.
AI.method: The authors define and distinguish two novel concepts: Agentic Technical Debt (a stock of design/governance liability from patching together prompts, memory, tool schemas, orchestration graphs, etc.) and Stochastic Tax (a flow of recurring operational cost from keeping probabilistic agent behavior within acceptable bounds). They propose lightweight dashboards and governance controls to operationalize visibility.
AI.result: Introduction of a clear debt-vs-tax framework: debt as accumulated liability stock, tax as recurring operating cost flow. Suggestion that both can be made visible through minimal governance infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: Agentic systems require distinct governance metrics beyond traditional software debt; distinguishing between liability stock (debt) and operating cost flow (tax) enables better management of production-grade agentic AI.

title: Qwen-VLA: Unifying Vision-Language-Action Modeling across Tasks, Environments, and Robot Embodiments
summary: Embodied intelligence is often studied through specialized models for individual tasks such as manipulation or navigation, resulting in fragmented capabilities and limited generalization across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments. In this work, we study whether heterogeneous embodied decision-making problems can be unified within a single vision-language-action model. We present Qwen-VLA, a unified embodied foundation model that extends Qwen's vision-language modeling stack from perception, understanding, and reasoning to continuous action and trajectory generation through a DiT-based action decoder. Qwen-VLA is trained with a large-scale joint pretraining recipe over diverse data sources, including robotics manipulation trajectories, human egocentric demonstrations, synthetic simulation data, vision-and-language navigation data, trajectory-centric supervision, and auxiliary vision-language data. To support multiple robot platforms, we introduce embodiment-aware prompt conditioning, where robot-specific textual descriptions specify the current embodiment and control convention. We further cast manipulation, navigation, and trajectory prediction into a unified action-and-trajectory prediction framework, enabling transferable visual grounding, spatial reasoning, and continuous action generation across robot morphologies, task families, and environments. Experiments on manipulation, navigation, and trajectory-centric benchmarks show consistent multi-task performance and out-of-distribution generalization under variations in scene layout, background, lighting, object configuration, and robot embodiment. Qwen-VLA-Instruct achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 73.7% on Simpler-WidowX, 86.1%/87.2% on RoboTwin-Easy/Hard, 69.0% OSR on R2R, 59.6% SR on RxR, 76.9% average OOD success in real-world ALOHA experiments, and 26.6% zero-shot success on DOMINO dynamic manipulation.

AI.tldr: Qwen-VLA unifies heterogeneous embodied tasks (manipulation, navigation, trajectory prediction) into a single vision-language-action model using a DiT-based action decoder and embodiment-aware prompt conditioning, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligence suffers from fragmented capabilities due to specialized models for individual tasks, limiting generalization across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments. The authors aim to unify heterogeneous embodied decision-making problems within a single vision-language-action model.
AI.method: Qwen-VLA extends Qwen's vision-language stack with a DiT-based action decoder for continuous action/trajectory generation. It uses a large-scale joint pretraining recipe over diverse data (robotics manipulation, human egocentric demos, synthetic data, VLN data, trajectory supervision, auxiliary VL data). Embodiment-aware prompt conditioning uses robot-specific textual descriptions to specify embodiment and control convention. Manipulation, navigation, and trajectory prediction are cast into a unified action-and-trajectory prediction framework.
AI.result: Qwen-VLA-Instruct achieves: 97.9% on LIBERO, 73.7% on Simpler-WidowX, 86.1%/87.2% on RoboTwin-Easy/Hard, 69.0% OSR on R2R, 59.6% SR on RxR, 76.9% average OOD success in real-world ALOHA experiments, and 26.6% zero-shot success on DOMINO dynamic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: A single unified vision-language-action model can handle heterogeneous embodied tasks across diverse robot morphologies, task families, and environments, with strong multi-task performance and out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Better Later Than Sooner: Neuro-Symbolic Knowledge Graph Construction via Ontology-grounded Post-extraction Correction
summary: Question answering (QA) is a core challenge in AI, particularly for complex queries requiring multi-hop reasoning across documents, or symbolic operations like aggregation or exhaustive listing. Retrieval-augmented generation has become the dominant approach to QA, with recent graph-based variants addressing part of these issues by organizing knowledge to better support compositional questions. However, most textual graph-based RAG methods still lack the structure needed for symbolic operations useful to answer complex questions reliably. This motivates symbolic graph-based approaches, which extract knowledge graphs (KGs) whose relations are logic predicates that enable SQL-like querying. Yet these pipelines typically use LLMs for KG extraction, which can introduce consistency issues, where extracted facts may violate commonsense ontology constraints. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework for ontology-grounded KG construction combining open-domain extraction, embedding-based canonicalization of types and predicates, and targeted LLM-based correction of ontology violations. By deferring corrections to a post-extraction stage, our method avoids repeated LLM calls, substantially reducing token usage while improving KG consistency and preserving downstream QA quality. Finally, we show that the extracted KGs are well suited for symbolic querying by measuring the occurrence of SPARQL graph patterns.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework for ontology-grounded knowledge graph extraction that improves KG consistency and reduces token usage by deferring LLM-based corrections to a post-extraction stage, while preserving downstream QA quality and enabling symbolic SPARQL querying.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based RAG methods lack structure for reliable symbolic operations (e.g., aggregation, exhaustive listing) needed for complex QA. Symbolic graph-based approaches using LLM-extracted KGs suffer from consistency issues where facts violate commonsense ontology constraints, and repeated LLM calls are expensive.
AI.method: The proposed neuro-symbolic framework combines: (1) open-domain KG extraction, (2) embedding-based canonicalization of types and predicates, and (3) targeted LLM-based correction of ontology violations in a post-extraction stage, avoiding repeated LLM calls during extraction.
AI.result: The method reduces token usage substantially, improves KG consistency, and preserves downstream QA quality. Extracted KGs are shown to be well-suited for symbolic querying via measurement of SPARQL graph pattern occurrences.
AI.conclusion: Deferring ontology-grounded corrections to a post-extraction stage is an effective strategy for building consistent KGs that support symbolic querying for complex QA, without the high cost of online LLM-based correction during extraction.

title: Gaze2Act: Gaze-Conditioned Vision-Language-Action Policies for Interactive Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown strong potential for robot learning by following language instructions. However, in practice, language alone is often insufficient to precisely convey human intent. It is difficult to describe which exact object to interact with among similar candidates, where to act on the object, or how the target may change during execution. To address this limitation, we propose Gaze2Act, a novel VLA framework that leverages human gaze as a dynamic and intuitive intent signal for complex interactive manipulation. Gaze2Act first bridges the ego-exo view gap by mapping first-person gaze into the robot's perspective through cross-view semantic matching, producing both an object mask and a gaze point for coarse-to-fine target specification. These cues are then integrated into the policy through perception-level prompting and action-level conditioning, allowing the robot to attend to relevant regions and execute precise interactions under dynamic intent. In a systematic evaluation across seven task categories and 16 real-robot tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid, Gaze2Act achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intent accuracy and task success rate. It notably outperforms baselines in object disambiguation, fine-grained interaction, and dynamic intent steering. These results demonstrate that human gaze provides a natural, low-burden, and highly expressive modality for human-in-the-loop VLA control.

AI.tldr: Gaze2Act is a VLA framework that uses human gaze as an intent signal for robot manipulation, mapping first-person gaze to robot perspective via cross-view semantic matching, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 16 real-robot tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Language alone is insufficient to precisely convey human intent in robot learning—difficulties include disambiguating similar objects, specifying action locations, and tracking dynamic targets.
AI.method: Gaze2Act bridges the ego-exo view gap by mapping first-person gaze to robot perspective via cross-view semantic matching, producing object masks and gaze points for coarse-to-fine target specification. These cues are integrated through perception-level prompting and action-level conditioning.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across 7 task categories and 16 real-robot tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid, outperforming baselines in object disambiguation, fine-grained interaction, and dynamic intent steering.
AI.conclusion: Human gaze is a natural, low-burden, and highly expressive modality for human-in-the-loop VLA control.

title: Paper Agents, Paper Gains: An Empirical Analysis of DeFi Investment Agents
summary: DeFi investment agents, systems that use AI for autonomous on-chain trading, have attained over USD 3 billion in combined token valuations since late 2024. We survey over 1,900 AI-tagged crypto projects, filter to investment-focused agents, and curate 10 representative projects spanning strategy and observability dimensions. We then conduct a deep-dive architectural analysis of two prominent agent frameworks, ElizaOS and Virtuals Protocol, and a quantitative on-chain performance analysis of 11 Solana-based agent treasuries with publicly attributable trading activity, covering 925,323 token holders. We find that current deployments remain early and heterogeneous: (1) in our sample, many projects do not yet provide clear evidence of autonomous trade execution, and developer interviews suggest that many visible deployments remain basic API integrations; (2) agent treasuries retain over USD 30M in paper gains while token holders collectively lost USD 191.7M, with the top 1% of wallets capturing 81.4% of all gains (USD 1.81B); (3) token valuations are weakly connected to treasury fundamentals, with market-cap-to-AUM ratios exceeding 10,000x versus below 1x for established DeFi protocols; and (4) aggregate user gains peaked at USD 2.4B before declining to net losses, with median returns negative on every platform and tokens declining 93% on average from all-time highs. We interpret these outcomes as characteristic of a permissionless, first-generation market in which open infrastructure enables rapid experimentation but also allows naive or speculative agents to launch before robust standards for autonomy, performance, and stakeholder alignment emerge. We therefore propose a maturity framework along three dimensions: autonomous execution, risk-adjusted profitability, and stakeholder alignment, to characterize the gap between current deployments and future investment-grade agent systems.

AI.tldr: A survey of over 1,900 AI-crypto projects reveals that current DeFi investment agents remain early-stage, with most lacking true autonomous execution; agent treasuries hold $30M+ in paper gains while token holders lost $191.7M, with extreme wealth concentration (top 1% capturing 81.4% of gains), and a maturity framework is proposed along autonomy, profitability, and alignment dimensions.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the emerging landscape of AI-powered DeFi investment agents, which have rapidly grown to $3B+ in combined token valuations, and assess whether they deliver on their promise of autonomous, profitable trading.
AI.method: Surveyed 1,900+ AI-tagged crypto projects, filtered to investment-focused agents, curated 10 representative projects; conducted deep-dive architectural analysis of two frameworks (ElizaOS, Virtuals Protocol); performed quantitative on-chain analysis of 11 Solana-based agent treasuries covering 925,323 token holders.
AI.result: (1) Many projects lack clear evidence of autonomous trade execution; (2) agent treasuries show $30M+ paper gains but token holders lost $191.7M, top 1% captured 81.4% of gains ($1.81B); (3) market-cap-to-AUM ratios exceed 10,000x vs. <1x for established DeFi; (4) aggregate user gains peaked at $2.4B then declined to net losses, median returns negative on all platforms, tokens declined 93% on average from ATH.
AI.conclusion: Current DeFi investment agent market is a permissionless first-generation system with rapid experimentation but lacking standards for autonomy, performance, and stakeholder alignment; propose a maturity framework along three dimensions (autonomous execution, risk-adjusted profitability, stakeholder alignment) to characterize the path toward investment-grade agent systems.

title: A Heterogeneous Architecture for Robot RL Beyond GPU-Dominant Paradigms
summary: Simulation-based RL for contemporary robot control is increasingly organized around GPU-resident simulation: physics, rollout collection, and learning are placed on a single GPU-centric execution path. This paradigm has greatly improved training speed, but it has also encouraged a default assumption that efficient training requires physics to reside on the GPU. We revisit this assumption. Our view is that, in simulation-dominated robot control, the essential question is not which processor runs physics, but whether simulation throughput, policy learning, and runtime synchronization form an efficient end-to-end loop. We present UniLab, a heterogeneous CPU-simulation / GPU-learning architecture that decouples CPU-parallel simulation from GPU policy updates through a unified runtime for data movement, buffering, and synchronization. UniLab is implemented as a complete and extensible training system using MuJoCoUni and MotrixSim CPU-batched physics backends, supporting PPO, SAC, FlashSAC, TD3, and APPO.
