On representative simulation-based robot control tasks, UniLab improves end-to-end training efficiency by 3--10$\times$ under the same hardware configuration, while reducing dependence on the NVIDIA CUDA-based software stack and supporting cross-platform execution on the Apple macOS platform and the AMD ROCm and Intel XPU accelerator backends. These results show that GPU simulation is an effective path to efficient training, but not a necessary one, broadening the practical system choices available for robot RL training. Project page: https://github.com/unilabsim/UniLab.

AI.tldr: UniLab is a heterogeneous CPU-simulation / GPU-learning architecture that decouples simulation from policy updates, achieving 3-10× training speedup over GPU-resident simulation approaches while reducing CUDA dependency and supporting cross-platform execution.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the default assumption that efficient robot RL training requires GPU-resident physics simulation, arguing that end-to-end throughput of the simulation-learning loop matters more than where physics executes.
AI.method: UniLab uses a heterogeneous architecture with CPU-parallel simulation (via MuJoCoUni and MotrixSim backends) and GPU policy learning, connected through a unified runtime that manages data movement, buffering, and synchronization between CPU and GPU.
AI.result: UniLab achieves 3-10× end-to-end training efficiency improvement over GPU-resident simulation under the same hardware, supports multiple RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, FlashSAC, TD3, APPO), and runs on Apple macOS, AMD ROCm, and Intel XPU platforms beyond NVIDIA CUDA.
AI.conclusion: GPU simulation is an effective but not necessary path for efficient robot RL training; heterogeneous CPU-simulation/GPU-learning architectures broaden practical system choices available to the community.

title: ReasonOps: Operator Segmentation for LLM Reasoning Traces
summary: Chain-of-thought traces from large reasoning models can span tens of thousands of tokens, yet we lack a vocabulary for describing their internal structure. Previous methods developed to analyze chain-of-thought traces are either too rigid or not expressive enough, failing to capture features across domains and models. To remedy this, we develop ReasonOps, an unsupervised, expressive method for annotating chain-of-thought traces, providing succinct universal operators. Using ReasonOps, we analyze 44,662 traces from 12 thinking LLMs spanning 6 families across 8 reasoning benchmarks and discover that they share a common compositional structure: 7 recurring reasoning operators -- discourse-level moves such as backtracking, inferring, and hypothesizing -- that emerge from unsupervised clustering of sentence-initial 3-token pivots. These operators appear across every model family and benchmark domain, confirmed by three independent LLM judges who classify held-out samples at 70 -76% accuracy. We analyze the structure of operators on easy vs. hard problems, revealing that reflective operators are more helpful on hard problems and harm performance on easy problems. Operator sequences are highly model-identifying: a classifier trained on operator distributions alone recovers the source model with macro-AUC, revealing that each model family has a distinctive reasoning fingerprint. Structural operator features predict within-problem answer correctness well above baselines. Classifiers built on these operators reach WP-AUC and on AIME specifically. ReasonOps further enables early quality estimation well before the trace completes: we predict at WP-AUC for only 50% of the trace. The ReasonOps pipeline is unsupervised and annotation-free, enabling deep insights into LLM reasoning traces as well as strong downstream results on model identification and correctness prediction.

AI.tldr: ReasonOps is an unsupervised method that annotates chain-of-thought traces with 7 recurring reasoning operators (e.g., backtracking, inferring, hypothesizing) derived from clustering sentence-initial 3-token pivots. Analyzing 44,662 traces across 12 LLMs and 8 benchmarks reveals a universal compositional structure. These operators enable model identification (macro-AUC), correctness prediction (WP-AUC), and early quality estimation (WP-AUC at 50% trace), with reflective operators found more helpful on hard problems and harmful on easy ones.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought traces from large reasoning models can be extremely long (tens of thousands of tokens), yet there is no existing vocabulary or expressive method for describing their internal structure. Prior methods are either too rigid or not expressive enough to capture features across different domains and models.
AI.method: ReasonOps is an unsupervised, annotation-free pipeline that identifies recurring reasoning operators by clustering sentence-initial 3-token pivots from chain-of-thought traces. The approach was applied to 44,662 traces from 12 thinking LLMs across 6 model families and 8 reasoning benchmarks, yielding 7 universal operators. Validation was performed using three independent LLM judges classifying held-out samples (70-76% accuracy).
AI.result: Seven recurring reasoning operators (discourse-level moves like backtracking, inferring, hypothesizing) emerged across all model families and benchmark domains. Classifiers using operator distributions recover source models with macro-AUC, and structural operator features predict answer correctness at WP-AUC (on AIME). Early quality estimation achieves WP-AUC with only 50% of the trace. Reflective operators are more beneficial on hard problems but harm performance on easy problems.
AI.conclusion: ReasonOps provides a universal, annotation-free method for deep structural analysis of LLM reasoning traces, enabling model identification, correctness prediction, and early quality estimation. The discovered compositional structure offers new insights into how reasoning models operate across domains and difficulty levels.

title: RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving
comment: The first two authors contributed equally
summary: The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable construction of high-quality reasoning-centric unexpected scenarios, we propose an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework, comprising agents for seed task generation and verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation. Using the pipeline, we curated 30 diverse seed tasks and 208 tasks with mutations and graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning. We benchmark popular robot policies, pre-trained VLAs, and oracle-state planners. Our results reveal a significant performance gap: while pre-trained VLAs exhibit preliminary success on seed tasks after single-task fine-tuning, they struggle to perform on mutated tasks, implying their brittleness in manipulation tasks requiring reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments. Project page is available at https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/RoboWits.

AI.tldr: RoboWits is a bi-manual robotic benchmark for evaluating cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness under unexpected conditions, using an automated multi-agent pipeline to generate tasks with mutations. Results show that current VLAs struggle with mutated tasks requiring reasoning and adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current robotic benchmarks focus on skill-level execution and lack systematic evaluation of higher-level cognitive reasoning capabilities needed for robots operating in real-world environments under unexpected challenges.
AI.method: Proposes an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework (seed generation, verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation) to create 30 seed tasks and 208 mutated tasks with graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning.
AI.result: Pre-trained VLAs show preliminary success on seed tasks after single-task fine-tuning but perform poorly on mutated tasks, revealing brittleness in reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments.
AI.conclusion: There exists a significant performance gap in current robot policies and pre-trained VLAs when faced with reasoning-centric, mutated manipulation tasks, indicating a need for more robust cognitive reasoning capabilities.

title: GTA: Generating Long-Horizon Tasks for Web Agents at Scale
comment: Published at Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: Web agents, which couple language models with browsing and tool-use capabilities, show promise as open web assistants. Yet progress is increasingly limited by the lack of scalable, process-level supervision. Existing benchmarks are largely manually constructed, providing only coarse start-goal annotations without intermediate trajectories, while recent automatic generation efforts remain expensive, biased, and shallow. These limitations prevent reliable training and evaluation of agents that must generalize to realistic, multi-hop, cross-page tasks. We introduce a scalable framework, GTA, that integrates crawling, retrieval-based seeding, in-context generation, and automated quality control to produce realistic tasks paired with executable trajectories. This design decouples crawling from generation for greater efficiency, grounds tasks in the site graph to enforce compositionality, and ensures dense supervision through deterministic replays and systematic validation. We instantiate the pipeline on over 50 websites covering e-commerce, government, forums, and news, with multilingual and multi-hop coverage. The resulting benchmark reveals a significant human-agent performance gap and enables detailed diagnostics. Our contributions are three-fold: (i) formalizing multi-hop web-agent task generation, (ii) proposing an efficient and validated pipeline for automatic data creation, and (iii) releasing a dynamic benchmark with reproducible evaluation.

AI.tldr: GTA is a scalable framework for automatically generating realistic, multi-hop web agent tasks with executable trajectories by integrating crawling, retrieval-based seeding, in-context generation, and automated quality control, producing a benchmark across 50+ websites that reveals a significant human-agent performance gap.
AI.motivation: Current web agent benchmarks are limited by manual construction (coarse start-goal annotations without intermediate trajectories) or expensive, biased, and shallow automatic generation, preventing reliable training and evaluation of agents that must generalize to realistic multi-hop cross-page tasks.
AI.method: GTA integrates four components: (1) crawling to obtain site structure, (2) retrieval-based seeding to ground tasks in the site graph, (3) in-context generation to produce tasks paired with executable trajectories, and (4) automated quality control via deterministic replays and systematic validation. The design decouples crawling from generation for efficiency and enforces compositionality through site graph grounding.
AI.result: The pipeline was instantiated on over 50 websites (e-commerce, government, forums, news) with multilingual and multi-hop coverage. The resulting benchmark reveals a significant performance gap between humans and agents, and enables detailed diagnostic analysis.
AI.conclusion: Three contributions: (i) formalizing multi-hop web-agent task generation, (ii) proposing an efficient and validated pipeline for automatic data creation, and (iii) releasing a dynamic benchmark with reproducible evaluation.

title: DynaFLIP: Rethinking Robotics Perception via Tri-Modal-Dynamics Guided Representation
summary: Robot manipulation critically depends on perception that preserves the action-relevant aspects of a scene. Yet most robot learning pipelines are built upon visual encoders pre-trained for static recognition or vision-language alignment, leaving motion understanding to downstream policies. We introduce DynaFLIP, a dynamics-aware multimodal pre-training framework that pushes motion understanding upstream into perception. We construct image-language-3D flow triplets from heterogeneous human and robot videos, and use these triplets as training-time supervision to shape an image-only encoder. Our key idea is to encourage the three modalities to span a small simplex volume in the shared hyperspherical space -- a smaller simplex volume indicating stronger alignment. To avoid the geometric ambiguity and trivial collapse of naive volume minimization, we combine simplex-volume minimization with a cosine regularizer and a contrastive objective. Our analyses show that DynaFLIP focuses on control-relevant regions critical for manipulation. The resulting dynamics-aware representations serve as reusable visual backbones and consistently outperform baselines across diverse downstream policies, including VLAs. We validate this across diverse simulation and real-world setups, with gains reaching +22.5% under out-of-distribution scenarios. Our results suggest that robot generalization improves when visual representations are trained to encode not just what is present, but how the world changes under action.

AI.tldr: DynaFLIP is a dynamics-aware multimodal pre-training framework that uses image-language-3D flow triplets to train visual encoders that understand motion, achieving up to +22.5% improvement in out-of-distribution robot manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Most robot visual encoders are pre-trained for static recognition or vision-language alignment, leaving motion understanding to downstream policies. This disconnect limits generalization, especially under distribution shifts.
AI.method: Constructs image-language-3D flow triplets from heterogeneous human/robot videos; uses simplex-volume minimization with a cosine regularizer and contrastive objective to align three modalities in a shared hyperspherical space, encoding dynamics into an image-only encoder.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms baselines across diverse simulation and real-world setups, with gains of +22.5% under out-of-distribution scenarios; dynamics-aware representations serve as reusable backbones and improve VLAs.
AI.conclusion: Robot generalization improves significantly when visual representations encode not just static scene content but also how the world changes under action.

title: BenchTrace: A Benchmark for Testing Reflection Ability and Controlled Evolution in LLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents improve over time by reflecting on past failures, but existing evaluation is limited in two ways: it measures only task scores, leaving reflection quality unknown, and it relies on agents' own episode runs, offering no mechanism to target specific failure patterns. We present \textbf{BenchTrace}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolution ability in LLM agents. BenchTrace is built on a snapshot-reflection dataset of 1,821 annotated episodes spanning six diverse tasks, and comprises a \textbf{Reflection Evaluation} that probes failure identification through targeted QA tasks, and an \textbf{Evolution Evaluation} that tests whether past failure experience translates into avoidance behavior in a controlled self-evolution simulation. Building on BenchTrace, we propose \textbf{failure avoidance rate (FAR)}, a new evaluation metric measuring the fraction of test cases in which the agent successfully avoids the target failure instance. Experiments with Qwen3-32B and GPT-4.1 reveal that both models fall below a 30\% end-to-end pass rate on reflection evaluation, with diagnosis as the primary bottleneck. Evolution evaluation shows that self-evolution methods generally improve FAR over the non-evolving baseline, but agents forget early lessons as noise episodes accumulate, and agents fail to generalize their reflections beyond the specific context, causing negative transfer across task contexts. Our correlation analysis further reveals that only a fully correct reflection is strongly associated with higher FAR. BenchTrace exposes concrete limits of current self-evolution approaches and provides a controlled, model-agnostic framework for targeted evaluation.

AI.tldr: BenchTrace is a benchmark for evaluating self-evolution in LLM agents, comprising 1,821 annotated episodes across six tasks. It introduces Reflection Evaluation (targeted QA on failure identification) and Evolution Evaluation (controlled simulation of failure avoidance), plus a new metric FAR (failure avoidance rate). Experiments with Qwen3-32B and GPT-4.1 show both models under 30% pass rate on reflection, with diagnosis as the main bottleneck; self-evolution improves FAR but suffers from forgetting and negative transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of self-evolving agents only measures task scores, leaving reflection quality unknown, and relies on agents' own episode runs without targeting specific failure patterns.
AI.method: Built a snapshot-reflection dataset of 1,821 annotated episodes across six tasks; proposes Reflection Evaluation (QA-based failure identification) and Evolution Evaluation (controlled self-evolution simulation); introduces FAR metric measuring failure avoidance rate.
AI.result: Both Qwen3-32B and GPT-4.1 achieve <30% end-to-end pass rate on reflection evaluation; diagnosis is the primary bottleneck. Self-evolution improves FAR over baselines, but agents forget early lessons as noise episodes accumulate and fail to generalize reflections, causing negative transfer.
AI.conclusion: BenchTrace reveals concrete limits of current self-evolution approaches: poor reflection diagnosis, forgetting over time, and lack of generalization. It provides a controlled, model-agnostic evaluation framework.

title: Tailoring the Curriculum: Student-Centered Reasoning Distillation via Dynamic Data-Model Compatibility
summary: Reasoning distillation transfers complex reasoning abilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller ones, yet its success depends on how well the training data align with the student model. This paper introduces the Data-Model Compatibility (DMC) metric, which can be used to assess the suitability of a dataset for reasoning distillation on a student model. DMC provides an assessment by jointly considering data quality, relative difficulty, and student capability. We validated the effectiveness of DMC from two perspectives: (1) DMC exhibits a strong correlation with reasoning distillation performance; and (2) using DMC as the criterion for data selection leads to improved reasoning distillation performance. Both findings are consistently demonstrated across multiple student models and tasks. Moreover, since the DMC of each dataset dynamically changes during training, our experiments demonstrate that dynamically selecting datasets based on DMC can further enhance performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Data-Model Compatibility (DMC) metric to assess dataset suitability for reasoning distillation in smaller student models, shows it correlates with distillation performance and improves results when used for data selection, including dynamic selection during training.
AI.motivation: Reasoning distillation's success depends on how well training data aligns with the student model, but there was no effective metric to assess this compatibility beforehand.
AI.method: The authors propose DMC, a metric jointly considering data quality, relative difficulty, and student capability. Validated by (1) correlation with distillation performance and (2) using DMC as data selection criterion, including dynamic selection during training.
AI.result: DMC strongly correlates with reasoning distillation performance; using DMC for data selection improves distillation results; dynamically selecting datasets based on DMC during training further enhances performance.
AI.conclusion: DMC is an effective metric for assessing and improving dataset-student model compatibility in reasoning distillation, with dynamic selection yielding additional gains.

title: Planning with the Views via Scene Self-Exploration
summary: Can VLMs predict how each camera move changes the view, and plan many such moves ahead? We call this capability view planning, requiring (1)understanding how a single action transforms the view, and (2)composing many such transformations across multi-turn plans to identify a target view. We probe both abilities in our proposed ViewSuite, a 3D point-cloud environment on real ScanNet scenes. Across 13 frontier VLMs, a critical planning gap emerges: they possess basic view-action knowledge but fail to compose it across multi-turn plans, with the gap widening as viewpoint distance grows. To close this gap, we propose an iterative framework that alternates self-exploration with view graph distillation. The key insight is that all exploration trajectories, regardless of their outcome, collectively form a view graph that compactly captures how viewpoints connect across a scene. Distilling this graph into diverse supervised tasks reshapes the policy distribution and overcomes the sparse rewards that stall pure RL. This improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 2.5% to 47.8% on interactive view planning, surpassing GPT-5.4 Pro (18.5%) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (21.4%). Self-exploration emerges as a promising path toward VLMs that can actively reason and plan in 3D space.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that VLMs have basic view-action knowledge but fail to compose it across multi-turn plans for view planning. It introduces ViewSuite (a 3D point-cloud benchmark on ScanNet) and proposes an iterative self-exploration + view graph distillation framework that boosts Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 2.5% to 47.8%, surpassing GPT-5.4 Pro (18.5%) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (21.4%).
AI.motivation: Current VLMs lack the ability to plan multiple camera moves ahead in 3D space, i.e., they understand single view transformations but cannot compose them across multi-turn plans to reach a target view. The paper aims to probe and close this planning gap.
AI.method: (1) ViewSuite: a 3D point-cloud environment built on real ScanNet scenes for evaluating view planning. (2) An iterative framework alternating self-exploration (collecting trajectories regardless of outcome) with view graph distillation (compressing all trajectories into a graph capturing viewpoint connectivity, then distilling it into diverse supervised tasks to reshape policy distribution and overcome sparse rewards).
AI.result: Across 13 frontier VLMs, a critical planning gap exists: basic view-action knowledge exists but multi-turn composition fails, worsening with distance. The proposed framework boosts Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 2.5% to 47.8% on interactive view planning, surpassing GPT-5.4 Pro (18.5%) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (21.4%).
AI.conclusion: Self-exploration combined with view graph distillation is a promising path toward VLMs that can actively reason and plan in 3D space, overcoming the multi-turn planning gap identified in existing models.

title: Rethinking Literature Search Evaluation: Deep Research Helps, and Human Citation Lists Are Not a Ground Truth
summary: We study large-scale literature search from two complementary angles: improving the retrieval pipeline, and stress-testing the human reference list as an evaluation target. First, we implement a Deep Research pipeline that processes the full query paper and expands the retrieved results breadth-first along their bibliographies, and show that it substantially outperforms vanilla API-only search, raising recall on RollingEval-Jun25 (a 250-paper literature-search benchmark) from below 20% to above 80%. Second, we use a neutral LLM-as-a-judge to determine if human references are sound ground truth for the task. We find significant limitations: only 51% of human citations are judged moderately relevant or higher, against 86--88% for the strongest AI-based re-rankers. We study this gap on the OpenAlex co-authorship graph, finding that humans are 2.5x more likely than the best AI re-rankers to cite a direct collaborator. Together, our results argue against single-axis literature-search evaluation: recall, topical-relevance scoring, ranked-list diversity, and a co-authorship-distance diagnostic each measure complementary properties of citation quality and should be reported jointly.

AI.tldr: This paper improves literature search via a Deep Research pipeline (breadth-first bibliography expansion, boosting recall from <20% to >80% on a 250-paper benchmark) and reveals that human reference lists are biased (only 51% moderately relevant vs. 86-88% for AI re-rankers; humans 2.5x more likely to cite collaborators), advocating for multi-axis evaluation (recall, relevance, diversity, co-authorship distance).
AI.motivation: To improve large-scale literature search by (1) enhancing the retrieval pipeline beyond vanilla API search, and (2) critically examining whether human reference lists constitute a valid gold standard for evaluation, given potential citation biases.
AI.method: A Deep Research pipeline that processes the full query paper and performs breadth-first expansion along bibliographies; evaluation uses RollingEval-Jun25 (250-paper benchmark) and an LLM-as-a-judge to assess relevance of human citations vs. AI re-rankers, complemented by analysis on the OpenAlex co-authorship graph.
AI.result: Deep Research pipeline raises recall from <20% to >80%. Only 51% of human citations are judged moderately relevant or higher vs. 86-88% for top AI re-rankers. Humans are 2.5x more likely than AI to cite direct collaborators.
AI.conclusion: Single-axis literature-search evaluation is insufficient; recall, topical relevance, ranked-list diversity, and co-authorship-distance diagnostic each capture complementary properties and should be reported jointly.

title: Surfacing Isolated Learners with Outcome-Independent Mediation of Feedback between Teachers and Students Using AI
comment: Accepted to HAI-Agency Workshop on Orchestrating Human and AI Agency for Proactive and Reflective Learning
summary: AI-augmented classrooms generate rich teacher and student feedback before graded outcomes become available, yet these signals can be difficult to translate into timely instructional decisions. We propose an interpretable decision layer: a transparent mechanism that ranks course topics requiring attention without using grades or post-hoc outcome labels. The approach combines three signals: student learning difficulty prevalence, disagreement between learner self-reports and observed difficulties, and unresolved teacher concerns. The output is a ranked set of topic priorities with per-topic decision records explaining each ranking. In one graduate CS course offering ($n=5$ instructor interviews; $n=279$ survey responses), prioritized topics aligned with instructor concerns (top-5 overlap 3/5; Spearman $ρ=0.80$) and student-reported topic difficulty ($ρ=0.46$, $p=.048$). Multi-signal integration also surfaced learners not identified through individual signal sources alone (AUC $=0.96$ vs. $0.91$ for gap prevalence alone). Reflective thinking, help-seeking, and self-efficacy provided additional evidence that student behavioral signals align with learning-related constructs. While preliminary, these findings suggest that transparent coordination mechanisms may help support human-AI co-agency when feedback is incomplete.

AI.tldr: A transparent decision layer ranks course topics needing attention by combining student difficulty prevalence, self-report vs. observed difficulty disagreement, and unresolved teacher concerns—without using grades—showing alignment with instructor concerns (ρ=0.80) and identifying at-risk learners (AUC=0.96).
AI.motivation: AI-augmented classrooms generate rich feedback before graded outcomes, but this feedback is difficult to translate into timely instructional decisions. The paper aims to create a transparent mechanism for prioritizing instructional attention without relying on grades or post-hoc labels.
AI.method: Three signals are combined: (1) student learning difficulty prevalence, (2) disagreement between learner self-reports and observed difficulties, and (3) unresolved teacher concerns. The output is a ranked set of topic priorities with per-topic decision records. Evaluated in one graduate CS course (n=5 instructor interviews; n=279 survey responses).
AI.result: Prioritized topics aligned with instructor concerns (top-5 overlap 3/5; Spearman ρ=0.80) and student-reported difficulty (ρ=0.46, p=.048). Multi-signal integration improved at-risk learner identification (AUC=0.96 vs. 0.91 for gap prevalence alone). Behavioral signals correlated with reflective thinking, help-seeking, and self-efficacy.
AI.conclusion: Transparent coordination mechanisms may help support human-AI co-agency when feedback is incomplete, though findings are preliminary.

title: DenseSteer: Steering Small Language Models towards Dense Math Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning abilities, while smaller models (<= 3B parameters) significantly underperform on multi-step reasoning tasks. Based on empirical analyses of the Qwen-2.5 model family on math reasoning benchmarks, we find that more proficient reasoning is associated with fewer reasoning steps but higher information density per step, a property we term Dense Reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we propose DenseSteer, a training-free inference-time steering framework that enhances small-model reasoning by modulating internal representations toward dense reasoning patterns. Experiments show that our method yields consistent accuracy improvements without increasing token-level Negative Log-Likelihood, highlighting dense reasoning as an effective structural approach to mathematical problem solving.

AI.tldr: DenseSteer improves small LLMs' math reasoning by steering internal representations toward denser reasoning patterns, where each step carries more information with fewer total steps, yielding accuracy gains without hurting likelihood.
AI.motivation: Small models (≤3B parameters) significantly underperform on multi-step reasoning tasks compared to larger models, and the authors aim to bridge this gap by identifying and leveraging dense reasoning patterns observed in more proficient models.
AI.method: The paper proposes DenseSteer, a training-free inference-time steering framework that modulates the internal representations of small models toward dense reasoning patterns (fewer steps, higher information density per step).
AI.result: DenseSteer yields consistent accuracy improvements on math reasoning benchmarks without increasing token-level Negative Log-Likelihood.
AI.conclusion: Dense reasoning is an effective structural approach to mathematical problem solving, and steering toward this pattern can enhance small-model performance without additional training.

title: Provably Secure Agent Guardrail
summary: As large language models transition from bounded generative engines to agents with expansive execution privileges, AI going out of control precipitates a fundamental crisis in artificial intelligence security. Existing defense architectures heavily rely on empirical semantic guardrails and probabilistic large model adjudicators, mechanisms that fail to provide deterministic security lower bounds when facing complex semantic symbol decoupling attacks. To overcome this empirical semantic guardrail dilemma, this paper proposes a new security paradigm for agents based on the fundamental limitations of logical reasoning. Based on this paradigm, we further introduce an executable Proof-Constrained Action (ePCA) framework with a neural symbolic isolation architecture. This framework abandons semantic trust in natural language, forcing agents to losslessly formalize their intentions into first-order logical mathematical constraints before performing physical operations. Empirical evaluations of macroscopic and microscopic two-dimensional dynamic adversarial systems demonstrate that our formal verification mechanism achieves zero attack success rate and zero false positive rate across the evaluated scenarios, with extremely low computational latency. This research provides a conditional formal foundation under explicit system assumptions and an engineering paradigm for constructing the underlying defense foundation for future intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ePCA, a neural-symbolic framework that forces AI agents to formalize intentions into first-order logic constraints before acting, achieving zero attack success rate against adversarial attacks while maintaining low computational latency.
AI.motivation: Existing defense mechanisms (semantic guardrails, probabilistic LLM adjudicators) cannot provide deterministic security lower bounds against complex semantic symbol decoupling attacks as LLMs become agents with expansive execution privileges.
AI.method: The ePCA framework employs a neural symbolic isolation architecture that abandons semantic trust in natural language, requiring agents to losslessly formalize intentions into first-order logical mathematical constraints before executing physical operations.
AI.result: In macroscopic and microscopic two-dimensional dynamic adversarial evaluations, the formal verification mechanism achieves zero attack success rate and zero false positive rate across all scenarios with extremely low computational latency.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a conditional formal foundation under explicit system assumptions and an engineering paradigm for constructing the underlying defense foundation for future intelligent systems.

title: OpenClawBench: Benchmarking Process-side Anomalies in Real-world Agent Execution Trajectories
summary: Task success can hide process anomalies in real-world agent executions. An agent may pass the final task oracle while still accumulating unresolved ambiguity, unsafe external writes, ignored errors, weakly grounded commitments, or capability-boundary overcommitment. We study this mismatch as the Outcome-Process Gap and introduce OpenClawBench, a large-scale dataset for measuring and supervising process-side anomalies in real agent execution processes. OpenClawBench is built from BFCL-driven OpenClaw sessions produced by 6 source models and contains 31,264 annotated trajectories. It aligns task-oracle outcomes with structured process evidence. FullTax converts the aligned trajectories into structured anomaly supervision: binary labels, supporting evidence, onset/span localization, severity, recoverability, and a 5-class anomaly taxonomy. Using OpenClawBench, we make the Outcome-Process Gap measurable. Among 31,135 oracle-passing executions, 2,904 are still labeled process-anomalous under FullTax. These results show that success-only evaluation misses a concrete class of process-side failures in real agent executions. A LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B detector trained on the high-confidence FullTax supervised pool reaches binary F1=0.729 on the cleaner-labels held-out test split. Together, OpenClawBench turns real agent execution logs into auditable and reusable supervision for studying, diagnosing, and operationally monitoring runtime agent reliability.

AI.tldr: OpenClawBench is a large-scale dataset (31,264 annotated trajectories) exposing the Outcome-Process Gap—where agent tasks pass final oracles yet harbor process anomalies. FullTax provides structured anomaly supervision. Among 31,135 oracle-passing executions, 2,904 are process-anomalous. A LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B detector achieves binary F1=0.729 on held-out test data.
AI.motivation: Task success can mask process anomalies (e.g., unresolved ambiguity, unsafe writes, ignored errors) in real-world agent executions, creating a mismatch between outcome and process quality that prior evaluation methods overlook.
AI.method: Built from BFCL-driven OpenClaw sessions from 6 source models; produces 31,264 annotated trajectories aligning task-oracle outcomes with structured process evidence via FullTax (binary labels, evidence, onset/span localization, severity, recoverability, 5-class taxonomy).
AI.result: Among 31,135 oracle-passing executions, 2,904 are process-anomalous. A LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B detector achieves binary F1=0.729 on the cleaner-labels held-out test split.
AI.conclusion: Success-only evaluation misses concrete process-side failures in real agent executions; OpenClawBench enables auditable, reusable supervision for studying and monitoring runtime agent reliability.

title: When and How Human Curation Backfires: Preference Alignment under Multi-Model Self-Consuming Loop
summary: Foundation models are increasingly trained on synthetic data generated by prior model iterations rather than exclusively on real data. This self-consuming training paradigm can lead to model collapse, divergence, or bias amplification. Recent work (Ferbach et al., 2024) shows that incorporating human curation into the loop can steer a self-consuming model toward human-aligned behavior, but these analyses focus on a single, isolated model that solely consumes its own outputs. In practice, however, models often interact and train on input-output pairs produced by other models. This paper studies self-consuming training in the multi-model regime. We first formalize a framework for interacting self-consuming models and characterize when the resulting dynamical system converges to a stable point. We then examine how human curation of one model affects its own alignment (self-influence) and how such effects propagate to other models (cross-influence). Unlike isolated settings where human curation always enhances model alignment, we show that cross-model interactions can dampen or even invert this effect, ultimately degrading long-term alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper studies self-consuming training in multi-model regimes, showing that human curation of one model can have counterproductive cross-influence effects on other models, potentially degrading long-term alignment unlike in isolated settings.
AI.motivation: Prior work on self-consuming (synthetic data) training focused on isolated single models; in practice, models interact and train on outputs from other models, so understanding multi-model dynamics is crucial.
AI.method: The authors formalize a framework for interacting self-consuming models, characterize convergence conditions for the dynamical system, and analyze self-influence and cross-influence of human curation across models.
AI.result: Cross-model interactions can dampen or invert the alignment benefits of human curation that would be observed in isolated settings, ultimately degrading long-term alignment.
AI.conclusion: Human curation in multi-model self-consuming training loops does not guarantee improved alignment due to propagating cross-influence effects, highlighting the need for coordinated interventions across models.

title: Indexing the Unreadable: LLM-Native Recursive Construction and Search of Service Taxonomies
comment: Preprint. 8 pages main paper + appendix; 2 figures. Under submission to EMNLP 2026
summary: The era of the Internet of Agents (IoA) is taking shape: LLM agents are expected to fulfill user goals by orchestrating fast-growing populations of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, Agent-to-Agent (A2A) endpoints, reusable skills, and other LLM-callable services. Yet LLMs face a structural mismatch with this regime: effective context is a scarce resource that does not scale with the number of services. Concatenating thousands of service descriptions into a prompt overflows the context window, and even when the window is large enough, models systematically under-attend to information in the middle of long inputs, the well-documented Lost-in-the-Middle phenomenon. This is fundamentally a question of context management for service discovery. To address this, we propose an LLM-native progressive-disclosure scheme and its concrete instantiation, A2X (Agent-to-Anything service discovery): an LLM-driven pipeline that automatically organizes the registered services into a hierarchical taxonomy and walks it layer by layer at query time, so that every LLM call sees only a small candidate set highly relevant to the user query. This decouples effective-context scarcity from registry size and significantly reduces token consumption while improving retrieval accuracy. Compared to full-context dumping, A2X achieves a 6.2-point Hit Rate gain at one-ninth the prompt-token cost; compared to the state-of-the-art open-source embedding-based baseline, A2X improves Hit Rate by more than 20 points.

AI.tldr: A2X proposes an LLM-native progressive-disclosure scheme that hierarchically organizes service registries and walks through them layer by layer at query time, enabling effective service discovery without overwhelming context windows or suffering from Lost-in-the-Middle issues.
AI.motivation: LLMs face a structural mismatch with the emerging Internet of Agents (IoA) regime: effective context is scarce and does not scale with the number of services. Concatenating thousands of service descriptions overflows context windows, and models exhibit Lost-in-the-Middle under-attention even with large windows.
AI.method: A2X (Agent-to-Anything service discovery) is an LLM-driven pipeline that automatically organizes registered services into a hierarchical taxonomy and walks it layer by layer at query time, ensuring each LLM call sees only a small candidate set highly relevant to the user query.
AI.result: A2X achieves a 6.2-point Hit Rate gain over full-context dumping at one-ninth the prompt-token cost, and improves Hit Rate by more than 20 points over the state-of-the-art open-source embedding-based baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed progressive-disclosure scheme decouples effective-context scarcity from registry size, significantly reducing token consumption while improving retrieval accuracy for service discovery in the IoA setting.

title: CoHyDE: Iterative Co-Training of LLM Rewriter & Dense Encoder for Tool Retrieval
summary: Tool retrieval over large API catalogs is a core bottleneck for LLM agents: user queries arrive in colloquial, often underspecified language, while the catalog uses technical API vocabulary that no fixed encoder can bridge on its own. The two dominant training approaches, contrastive encoder fine-tuning and HyDE-style query expansion with a frozen LLM, address this problem from opposite ends and fail in complementary directions: the fine-tuned encoder excels when the query's surface form already matches the catalog but collapses when it does not, while zero-shot HyDE is more robust to underspecified queries yet generates catalog-unaware hypothetical descriptions that degrade retrieval when queries are well-formed. We introduce CoHyDE, an iterative procedure that trains the dense encoder and the LLM rewriter as a single co-evolving system: the encoder is retrained with InfoNCE on catalog-style hypothetical descriptions produced by the rewriter, and the rewriter is preference-aligned via DPO against the encoder's retrieval scores, with both sides warm-started on the tool catalog before the loop begins. On a ~10k tool subset of the ToolBench catalog, three rounds of CoHyDE improve over the strongest single-component baseline by +2.5 pp NDCG@5 on standard queries and +6.3 pp on held-out vague queries, with gains as large as +8 pp on the hardest vague tier. Ablations confirm that co-training is the key ingredient: using either component in isolation fails to match CoHyDE on both well-formed and vague queries, with losses of up to -8 pp on vague queries.

AI.tldr: CoHyDE is an iterative co-training framework where a dense encoder and an LLM rewriter are jointly optimized—encoder via InfoNCE on catalog-style query expansions and rewriter via DPO against retrieval scores—achieving up to +8 pp NDCG@5 improvements on vague queries over baselines on ToolBench's ~10k tool catalog.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches (contrastive encoder fine-tuning and HyDE-style query expansion) address the vocabulary mismatch between colloquial user queries and technical API catalogs from opposite ends but fail in complementary directions: fine-tuned encoders collapse on mismatched surface forms, while HyDE generates catalog-unaware descriptions that degrade retrieval on well-formed queries.
AI.method: CoHyDE iteratively trains a dense encoder (via InfoNCE loss) and an LLM rewriter (via DPO preference alignment against encoder retrieval scores) as a co-evolving system, with both components warm-started on the tool catalog before the iterative loop begins.
AI.result: On ToolBench's ~10k tool subset, CoHyDE improves NDCG@5 by +2.5 pp on standard queries and +6.3 pp on vague queries over the best single-component baseline, with up to +8 pp on the hardest vague tier. Ablations confirm co-training is essential; using either component alone loses up to -8 pp on vague queries.
AI.conclusion: Co-training the encoder and rewriter is the key ingredient for robust tool retrieval across both well-formed and underspecified queries, outperforming approaches that optimize either component in isolation.

title: Diagnosing Harmful Continuation in Answer-Correct Long-CoT Training Traces
summary: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces are widely used as supervision for reasoning-oriented LLM SFT, yet answer-correct traces can still lead to markedly different fine-tuning outcomes. We study post-conclusion continuation in answer-correct long-CoT data: a continuation where the answer appears sufficiently supported, but the trace continues with additional reasoning that remains in the supervised target. To test its training effect, we use a delete-only editor to construct answer-preserving suffix removal and compare CoT-based SFT on the original and processed traces. We observe improved SFT outcomes after removing the editor-identified post-conclusion continuation, suggesting that this continuation is harmful to training in our setting. We therefore refer to this empirically supported phenomenon as harmful continuation. Beyond this intervention, we further characterize the removed post-conclusion continuation through uncertainty and hidden-state progress. We observe persistent local uncertainty together with weakened terminal-directional progress, forming an uncertainty--geometry mismatch. Finally, we instantiate Harmful Continuation Cut (HCC), a lightweight boundary proxy that approximates the editor-identified post-conclusion continuation boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "harmful continuation" in long chain-of-thought training data—reasoning that continues after the answer is already supported—which degrades SFT outcomes. Removing this continuation improves performance, and the phenomenon is characterized by an uncertainty-geometry mismatch. A lightweight boundary proxy (HCC) is proposed to detect and cut these harmful continuations.
AI.motivation: Answer-correct long CoT traces can lead to different fine-tuning outcomes; the paper investigates whether certain segments of post-conclusion reasoning in these traces negatively affect SFT.
AI.method: (1) A delete-only editor constructs answer-preserving suffix removal; (2) CoT-based SFT is compared on original vs. processed traces; (3) Uncertainty and hidden-state progress metrics characterize removed continuations; (4) HCC boundary proxy is instantiated.
AI.result: Removing post-conclusion continuation improves SFT outcomes. The removed continuations exhibit persistent local uncertainty and weakened terminal-directional progress (uncertainty-geometry mismatch).
AI.conclusion: Post-conclusion continuation is harmful to CoT SFT; HCC provides a lightweight method to identify and remove it.

title: Entropy-KL Divergence-based Token Masking: A Novel Approach for Selective Fine-tuning of Large Language Models
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training paradigm for large language models. This paradigm provides a cold-start for RL exploration, avoiding the inefficiency of pure RL where on-policy sampling yields insufficient positive samples. However, in practice, existing approaches often use a small amount of data for SFT initialization compared to the RL phase, which can cause the model to fit the limited samples and shift away from its pre-trained distribution. This distribution shift impedes the model's ability to effectively explore during subsequent RL training. To address this challenge, we propose that in low-data regimes, SFT should prioritize activating task-relevant capabilities rather than memorizing specific content. Along this line, we propose EKSFT (Entropy-KL Selective Fine-Tuning), which selectively masks tokens that exhibit either high entropy or high KL divergence from a reference model. By excluding these high-uncertainty, distribution-shifting tokens from imitation, EKSFT injects task-specific knowledge while preserving the integrity of the model's pre-trained distribution. Empirical evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EKSFT consistently outperforms standard SFT. Further RL fine-tuning from the EKSFT model yields consistently better post-RL performance, indicating improved exploration for the RL stage. Our codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/MINE-USTC/EKSFT.

AI.tldr: EKSFT proposes selectively masking high-entropy and high-KL tokens during supervised fine-tuning to preserve pre-trained distribution, enabling better RL exploration and improved mathematical reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Standard SFT followed by RL uses limited SFT data, causing the model to overfit and shift away from its pre-trained distribution, which hinders effective exploration during subsequent RL training.
AI.method: EKSFT (Entropy-KL Selective Fine-Tuning) selectively masks tokens that exhibit either high entropy or high KL divergence from a reference model, excluding high-uncertainty, distribution-shifting tokens from imitation to inject task-specific knowledge while preserving pre-trained distribution integrity.
AI.result: EKSFT consistently outperforms standard SFT on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and subsequent RL fine-tuning from EKSFT yields better post-RL performance, indicating improved exploration.
AI.conclusion: In low-data regimes, SFT should prioritize activating task-relevant capabilities over memorizing specific content; EKSFT achieves this via selective token masking, leading to better downstream RL performance.

title: Rubric-Guided Process Reward for Stepwise Model Routing
summary: Stepwise model routing improves the efficiency of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by assigning each reasoning step to a suitable model. Recent methods formulate routing as a sequential decision process and train the router with reinforcement learning. However, although they model routing as a process, they still supervise the router with outcome rewards. Such rewards only reflect final answer correctness and fail to evaluate intermediate routing decisions, which can weaken performance and generalization. To address this gap, we propose RoRo, a rubric-guided process reward framework for stepwise model routing. RoRo first collects diverse routing trajectories and constructs preference pairs based on outcome, cost, and process quality. It then trains a Rubricor to generate a query-specific evaluation rubric and a Judge to score routing trajectories under this rubric through alternating optimization. The resulting process rewards are combined with outcome rewards to optimize the routing policy via GRPO. Experiments on five reasoning benchmarks under both same-family and cross-family settings show that RoRo consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves better accuracy and cost trade-offs.

AI.tldr: RoRo introduces rubric-guided process rewards to supervise stepwise model routing for LRMs, outperforming reinforcement learning methods that rely solely on outcome rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing stepwise model routing methods formulate routing as a sequential decision process but still supervise the router with outcome rewards (only reflecting final answer correctness), which fails to evaluate intermediate routing decisions and weakens performance and generalization.
AI.method: RoRo collects diverse routing trajectories, constructs preference pairs based on outcome, cost, and process quality, trains a Rubricor to generate query-specific evaluation rubrics, and trains a Judge to score routing trajectories under this rubric via alternating optimization. Process rewards are combined with outcome rewards to optimize the routing policy via GRPO.
AI.result: On five reasoning benchmarks under both same-family and cross-family settings, RoRo consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves better accuracy and cost trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Process-level supervision via rubrics is more effective than outcome-only rewards for training routers in stepwise model routing for LRMs.

title: ConMoE: Expert-Pool Consolidation via Prototype Reassignment for MoE Compression
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models reduce per-token computation but still require storing and serving all experts, making deployment memory-intensive. Existing post-training compression methods mainly shrink this cost by pruning experts or merging their weights. We formulate post-training MoE compression as expert-pool consolidation: retaining a smaller set of pretrained experts as reusable prototypes and deterministically remapping each original expert reference to one selected prototype. This view separates the reduced expert pool from the reuse structure that represents the original expert slots, and allows prototype sharing within local layer scopes while preserving the original router interface. We propose ConMoE, a train-free prototype remapping framework that selects retained experts using calibration-based contribution and replaceability signals, then redirects original expert calls to the selected prototypes without weight updates or post-compression fine-tuning. Experiments on three pretrained MoE language models show that ConMoE matches or outperforms strong pruning and merging baselines in several settings, achieving the best average score on deepseek-moe-16b-base at both 25% and 50% routed-expert reduction, while remaining competitive on Qwen3-30B-A3B and OLMoE-1B-7B-0125. Ablations indicate that deterministic reassignment is the most stable component, whereas broader cross-layer sharing and post-hoc weight fusion are model-dependent.

AI.tldr: ConMoE is a train-free post-training compression method for MoE language models that selects a subset of original experts as prototypes and deterministically remaps all expert references to them, reducing memory without weight updates or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: MoE language models require storing and serving all experts, making deployment memory-intensive despite reduced per-token computation. Existing post-training compression methods mainly prune experts or merge weights, but these approaches have limitations.
AI.method: ConMoE formulates compression as expert-pool consolidation: retain a smaller set of pretrained experts as reusable prototypes, then deterministically remap each original expert reference to one selected prototype using calibration-based contribution and replaceability signals. No weight updates or fine-tuning required.
AI.result: Matches or outperforms strong pruning and merging baselines on three pretrained MoE models (deepseek-moe-16b-base, Qwen3-30B-A3B, OLMoE-1B-7B-0125). Achieves best average score at both 25% and 50% routed-expert reduction on deepseek-moe-16b-base.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic reassignment is the most stable component of the framework, while cross-layer sharing and post-hoc weight fusion are model-dependent.

title: PassNet: Scaling Large Language Models for Graph Compiler Pass Generation
comment: Code and data available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PassNet
summary: Modern tensor compilers such as TorchInductor deliver substantial speedups on mainstream models, yet face a systematic performance ceiling on long-tail workloads -- our profiling shows that 43% of real-world subgraphs experience end-to-end slowdowns under default compilation. While LLMs offer a path toward automated optimization, existing efforts focus on standalone kernel generation. We argue that pass generation -- where LLMs author structured graph transformations that integrate directly into compiler pipelines -- is the more appropriate abstraction. We propose PassNet, the first large-scale ecosystem for LLM-based compiler pass generation, comprising: (1) PassNet-Dataset, over 18K unique computational graphs from 100K real-world models; and (2) PassBench, 200 curated long-tail fusible tasks (comprising 2,060 subgraphs in total) evaluated under the Error-aware Speedup Score (ES_t) -- a metric unifying correctness, stability, and performance -- with layered integrity defenses against systematic LLM exploitation. Experiments reveal that PassBench is both highly discriminative and genuinely unsaturated: the best frontier model trails TorchInductor by 37% in aggregate, yet on individual subgraphs LLMs achieve up to 3x speedup over the same compiler -- indicating that the bottleneck is consistency, not capability. Fine-tuning a small model on merely ~4K PassNet trajectories yields a 2.67x improvement approaching frontier-model performance, demonstrating substantial headroom and validating PassNet as live training infrastructure for advancing LLM-driven compiler optimization. All data, benchmarks, and tooling are publicly available.

AI.tldr: PassNet is the first large-scale ecosystem for LLM-based compiler pass generation, addressing the performance ceiling of modern tensor compilers on long-tail workloads. It includes a dataset of 18K+ computational graphs, a benchmark of 200 curated tasks, and an evaluation metric (ES_t) combining correctness, stability, and performance. Experiments show frontier LLMs trail TorchInductor by 37% on aggregate but achieve up to 3x speedup on individual subgraphs, while fine-tuning a small model on ~4K trajectories yields a 2.67x improvement, validating PassNet as live training infrastructure for LLM-driven compiler optimization.
AI.motivation: Modern tensor compilers (e.g., TorchInductor) suffer systematic performance degradation on long-tail workloads — 43% of real-world subgraphs experience end-to-end slowdowns under default compilation — yet existing LLM-based optimization efforts focus on standalone kernel generation rather than the more appropriate abstraction of compiler pass generation.
AI.method: PassNet introduces: (1) PassNet-Dataset with 18K+ unique computational graphs from 100K real-world models; (2) PassBench, 200 curated long-tail fusible tasks (2,060 subgraphs); (3) Error-aware Speedup Score (ES_t) metric unifying correctness, stability, and performance with layered integrity defenses against LLM exploitation; and (4) fine-tuning a small model on ~4K PassNet trajectories.
AI.result: The best frontier model trails TorchInductor by 37% in aggregate on PassBench. However, on individual subgraphs, LLMs achieve up to 3x speedup over the same compiler, indicating consistency (not capability) is the bottleneck. Fine-tuning a small model on ~4K trajectories yields a 2.67x improvement, approaching frontier-model performance.
AI.conclusion: PassBench is highly discriminative and genuinely unsaturated, revealing substantial headroom for LLM-driven compiler optimization. PassNet is validated as live training infrastructure for advancing this direction, with all data, benchmarks, and tooling publicly released.

title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
summary: We demonstrate that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from Claude 3 Sonnet, a production-scale language model, addressing the open question of whether dictionary learning methods scale beyond small transformers. We trained sparse autoencoders with up to 34 million features on the model's middle layer residual stream, using scaling laws to guide hyperparameter selection. The resulting features are multilingual and multimodal (generalizing to images despite text-only training), respond to both concrete instances and abstract discussions of concepts, and can be used to steer model behavior in ways consistent with their interpretations. We find features corresponding to famous entities and locations, as well as more abstract concepts like sarcasm or errors in code. We also identify features relevant to ways in which language models might cause harm--including features representing deception, power-seeking, sycophancy, and bias--and show that these causally influence model outputs when manipulated. Additionally, we conduct analyses of feature interpretability, geometry, and computational function. However, significant limitations remain: our suite of features is incomplete, and we lack rigorous methods for evaluating whether our features faithfully capture model computations.

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable, multilingual, multimodal features from Claude 3 Sonnet's middle layer (up to 34M features), including abstract concepts and safety-relevant features like deception and power-seeking, though limitations in completeness and evaluation methods remain.
AI.motivation: To address the open question of whether dictionary learning methods (sparse autoencoders) can scale beyond small transformers and extract interpretable features from production-scale language models.
AI.method: Trained sparse autoencoders with up to 34 million features on the middle layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, using scaling laws to guide hyperparameter selection.
AI.result: Features are multilingual, multimodal (generalize to images despite text-only training), respond to both concrete and abstract concepts, and causally influence model outputs when manipulated. Identified features for entities, locations, abstract concepts (sarcasm, code errors), and safety-relevant concepts (deception, power-seeking, sycophancy, bias).
AI.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders scale to production models and yield interpretable features with causal influence, but the feature set is incomplete and lacks rigorous faithfulness evaluation methods.

title: MiraBench: Evaluating Action-Conditioned Reliability in Robotic World Models
summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as scalable simulators for robot learning, yet current evaluations provide limited evidence that their predictions are reliable under the actions they condition on. Existing benchmarks largely emphasize visual fidelity, leaving unclear whether predicted futures are physically plausible, faithful to commanded actions, and calibrated to failure when actions should not succeed. We introduce \textsc{MiraBench}, a hierarchical benchmark that defines \emph{action-conditioned reliability} as a core evaluation target for robotic world models. MiraBench decomposes this target into three progressively demanding levels: \emph{Physics Adherence}, which evaluates reference-free physical consistency; \emph{Action-Following Fidelity}, which measures whether predictions respect task-relevant action inputs; and \emph{Optimism Bias Detection}, which probes the tendency to predict successful outcomes under failure-inducing actions. To support this evaluation, we curate a human-annotated corpus with over 16,000 judgments across tasks, failure categories, and leading world models. We evaluate 12 representative model configurations spanning vector-conditioned robotic world models, text-conditioned generative world models, open-weight systems, closed-source systems, and multiple model scales. Across this broad model landscape, MiraBench reveals three central findings: visual fidelity is a poor proxy for action fidelity; increasing model scale does not reliably improve action following; and optimism bias is pervasive across current systems. By shifting evaluation from appearance to action-conditioned reliability, MiraBench provides a diagnostic foundation for assessing and improving robotic world models as faithful simulators.

AI.tldr: MiraBench is a hierarchical benchmark for evaluating action-conditioned reliability in robotic world models, assessing physics adherence, action-following fidelity, and optimism bias across 12 model configurations. Key findings: visual fidelity ≠ action fidelity, scaling doesn't improve action following, and optimism bias is pervasive.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for robotic world models focus on visual fidelity rather than whether predictions are physically plausible, faithful to commanded actions, and calibrated to failure. This leaves a gap in evaluating whether these models are reliable as scalable simulators for robot learning.
AI.method: MiraBench defines three hierarchical levels: Physics Adherence (reference-free physical consistency), Action-Following Fidelity (respecting task-relevant action inputs), and Optimism Bias Detection (tendency to predict success under failure-inducing actions). It uses a human-annotated corpus of 16K+ judgments across tasks, failure categories, and 12 model configurations (vector-conditioned, text-conditioned, open/closed-source, multiple scales).
AI.result: Three central findings: (1) visual fidelity is a poor proxy for action fidelity; (2) increasing model scale does not reliably improve action following; (3) optimism bias (predicting success despite failure-inducing actions) is pervasive across all current systems.
AI.conclusion: MiraBench shifts evaluation from appearance-based metrics to action-conditioned reliability, providing a diagnostic foundation for assessing and improving robotic world models as faithful simulators for robot learning.

title: EvoMD-LLM: Learning the Language of Species Evolution in Reactive Molecular Dynamics
summary: While large language models (LLMs) excel at static scientific reasoning, they struggle to model the temporal structure of dynamic physical processes. We present EvoMD-LLM (Evolutionary Molecular Dynamics Large Language Model), a framework that reformulates species-level molecular dynamics as a symbolic temporal language modeling problem. Reactive MD trajectories are discretized into sequences of molecular events, where each token represents a chemical species augmented with its persistence duration, enabling standard autoregressive LLMs to learn compositional evolution over time through efficient fine-tuning. A key component of EvoMD-LLM is temporal scaffolding, which treats event duration as an explicit linguistic token and serves as a structured inductive bias, significantly reducing invalid or hallucinated molecular outputs compared to conventional sequence modeling approaches. We evaluate EvoMD-LLM on multiple temporal prediction tasks, achieving up to 66.14% accuracy and consistently outperforming sequential neural networks and language-based baselines. Beyond quantitative improvements, we qualitatively observe that the model is capable of generating interpretations for its own predictions by incorporating relevant chemical knowledge, even though it was not explicitly supervised with paired trajectory-explanation data. These results demonstrate that symbolic temporal language modeling provides an effective framework for grounding LLMs in dynamic physical simulations.

AI.tldr: EvoMD-LLM reformulates molecular dynamics as a symbolic temporal language modeling problem by discretizing trajectories into molecular event sequences with persistence durations, enabling LLMs to model dynamic physical processes through temporal scaffolding, achieving up to 66.14% accuracy on temporal prediction tasks while generating interpretable chemical explanations without explicit supervision.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at static scientific reasoning but fail to model the temporal structure of dynamic physical processes, motivating the need for a framework that grounds LLMs in time-evolving molecular simulations.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics trajectories are discretized into sequences of molecular events where each token is a chemical species with its persistence duration. Temporal scaffolding treats duration as an explicit linguistic token, serving as a structured inductive bias. Standard autoregressive LLMs are fine-tuned on these symbolic temporal sequences.
AI.result: Achieves up to 66.14% accuracy on temporal prediction tasks, outperforming sequential neural networks and language-based baselines. The model generates interpretable explanations incorporating chemical knowledge without explicit supervision on paired trajectory-explanation data.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic temporal language modeling provides an effective framework for grounding LLMs in dynamic physical simulations, reducing hallucinated outputs and enabling interpretable predictions.

title: Aligned but Fragile: Enhancing LLM Safety Robustness via Zeroth-Order Optimization
summary:
Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) aims to reduce harmful or unsafe behavior while preserving general utility. However, recent findings reveal that alignment effects can be fragile: lightweight post-alignment manipulations, such as parameter noise, activation noise, or quantization, can easily weaken the intended safety behavior. Prior efforts to improve robustness have primarily focused on data curation, modified alignment objectives, and safety-critical parameter identification, leaving the role of the optimizer itself largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we are the first to study the robustness of safety alignment from the perspective of the base optimizer. This optimizer-centric view naturally points to zeroth-order optimization, which provides a robustness-oriented signal by evaluating safety alignment under perturbations. Based on this insight, we propose a hybrid framework that first performs standard first-order safety alignment and then applies zeroth-order refinement to improve robustness. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that only a few zeroth-order refinement steps can enhance robustness while preserving safety alignment. We further improve the efficiency of zeroth-order refinement by exploiting its inherent perturbation-based evaluations to estimate layer-wise robustness sensitivity, enabling the refinement process to concentrate updates on robustness-critical layers with modest training overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper studies safety alignment robustness in LLMs from an optimizer-centric perspective, proposing a hybrid framework that combines first-order safety alignment with zeroth-order refinement to improve robustness against post-alignment manipulations while preserving safety. The method also uses perturbation-based evaluations to estimate layer-wise sensitivity for efficient refinement.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment for LLMs is fragile to lightweight post-alignment manipulations (e.g., parameter noise, activation noise, quantization). Prior robustness efforts focused on data curation, alignment objectives, and parameter identification, leaving the role of the optimizer largely unexplored.
AI.method: Proposes a hybrid framework: first standard first-order safety alignment, then zeroth-order refinement. Zeroth-order optimization evaluates safety under perturbations, providing robustness-oriented signals. Further improves efficiency by using perturbation-based evaluations to estimate layer-wise robustness sensitivity and concentrate updates on critical layers.
AI.result: Both theoretically and empirically, only a few zeroth-order refinement steps enhance robustness while preserving safety alignment, with modest training overhead due to layer-wise sensitivity-based efficiency improvements.
AI.conclusion: The optimizer itself is a crucial factor in safety alignment robustness; zeroth-order refinement is an effective and efficient complement to first-order alignment for improving robustness against post-alignment manipulations.

title: Architecture-Sensitive Supervised Fine-Tuning for Screen-Conditioned Action Prediction: A PiSAR Benchmark
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. PiSAR corpus and fine-tuned weights are proprietary to AprioriLabs; methodology and recipe released
summary: We benchmark three supervised fine-tuned models against frontier zero-shot baselines on a 661-row held-out slice of PiSAR (Persona, intent, Screen, Action, Rationale), a 12,929-tuple corpus of screen-anchored behavioural rationales curated from public app-store reviews, Pew American Trends Panel demographics, and the OPeRA shopper traces. Every model, frontier or fine-tuned, is evaluated on the same 661-row slice with the same scoring pipeline. Two findings. First, frontier zero-shot baselines (Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5) reach sem_sim 0.459 and 0.482 respectively; a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct reaches 0.783 and clears sem_sim >= 0.7 on 79% of rows, against 1-2% for either frontier baseline, a gap of 0.30 absolute on the same test set. Second, the same training data and recipe on Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT scores only 0.441, in the same band as the frontier zero-shot baselines rather than the fine-tuned Qwen. We read this as a recipe-vs-model mismatch: the reasoning-tuned high-parameter model resists displacement and would likely need either more data or a stronger fine-tuning method.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (sem_sim 0.783) dramatically outperforms frontier zero-shot baselines (Claude Opus 4.7/GPT-5.5, ~0.46-0.48) and a similarly fine-tuned Gemma-4-26B (0.441) on a held-out 661-row slice of PiSAR, revealing that recipe-model compatibility matters more than raw parameter count.
AI.motivation: To benchmark supervised fine-tuned models against frontier zero-shot baselines on behavioral rationale generation, and to investigate whether fine-tuning gains generalize across different model architectures.
AI.method: Authors curated PiSAR (12,929 tuples from app-store reviews, Pew surveys, and OPeRA shopper traces), held out 661 rows for evaluation, and compared three fine-tuned models (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT) against zero-shot frontier baselines (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5) using semantic similarity (sem_sim) scoring.
AI.result: Fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct achieved sem_sim 0.783 with 79% rows >= 0.7; frontier baselines scored 0.459-0.482 with only 1-2% rows >= 0.7; fine-tuned Gemma-4-26B scored only 0.441, matching zero-shot baselines rather than the Qwen fine-tuned model.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning yields substantial gains over zero-shot prompting on this task, but success is model-dependent: the reasoning-tuned high-parameter Gemma model resists displacement under the same recipe, indicating a recipe-vs-model mismatch that would require more data or a stronger fine-tuning method.

title: When Does Persona Prompting Actually Help? A Retrieval and Metric Analysis of Expert Role Injection in LLMs
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Submitted for peer review
summary: Persona prompting is widely used to steer large language models, yet its practical value remains unclear. Prior work often evaluates persona prompting using aggregate scores, making it difficult to determine whether expert-role prompting consistently improves response quality or instead changes responses along different quality dimensions. We study this question through a controlled comparison of four prompting conditions across 1,140 open-ended questions spanning 38 expert roles and six domains: no role prompt, a generic domain-expert prompt, embedding-based role retrieval, and a hybrid retrieval method combining embedding search with LLM-based role selection. Aggregate results show only small overall differences between conditions. However, metric-level analysis reveals a consistent tradeoff that aggregate averages obscure: role prompting systematically increases expertise depth while reducing clarity. These effects are highly conditional rather than universal. Role prompting performs best on advisory questions and in domains such as medicine and psychology, where structured expert framing and risk communication are intrinsically valuable. In contrast, baseline prompting performs better on conceptual and explanatory questions in finance, legal, science, and technology domains, where concise plain-language explanation is more important. We further show that hybrid retrieval significantly improves over embedding-only role selection, although better role retrieval does not eliminate the broader expertise-depth versus clarity tradeoff. Overall, our findings suggest that persona prompting primarily reshapes response characteristics rather than broadly improving capability, and that multi-metric evaluation is necessary for understanding its effects.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of persona prompting across 1,140 questions and 38 roles reveals that persona prompting consistently increases expertise depth at the cost of clarity, with effects being highly conditional—beneficial for advisory/medical/psychology questions but detrimental for conceptual/explanatory queries in finance, legal, science, and technology domains. Hybrid retrieval improves role selection but does not eliminate this tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluates persona prompting using aggregate scores, which obscures whether expert-role prompting consistently improves response quality or shifts responses along different quality dimensions. The authors aim to uncover these nuanced effects through fine-grained metric-level analysis.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of four prompting conditions (no role, generic domain-expert, embedding-based role retrieval, hybrid retrieval) across 1,140 open-ended questions spanning 38 expert roles and six domains, evaluated with multi-metric analysis.
AI.result: Small aggregate differences but systematic tradeoff revealed at metric level: role prompting increases expertise depth while reducing clarity. Effects are conditional—beneficial for advisory questions and medicine/psychology domains; detrimental for conceptual/explanatory questions in finance, legal, science, and technology. Hybrid retrieval improves over embedding-only but doesn't eliminate the tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: Persona prompting primarily reshapes response characteristics (expertise-clarity tradeoff) rather than broadly improving capability; multi-metric evaluation is essential for understanding its effects.

title: ReasonLight: A Multimodal Foundation Model-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning Framework for Zero-Shot Traffic Signal Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in traffic signal control (TSC). However, its reliance on predefined states limits responsiveness to observable open-world events that are absent from training data. IoT-enabled intersections provide heterogeneous observations from roadside sensors and cameras, creating opportunities to improve RL adaptability to such events. To this end, we propose ReasonLight, a multimodal foundation model-enhanced RL framework for zero-shot TSC.
