AI.tldr: This paper explores how data organization (ordering) impacts LLM training efficiency and performance, proposing four guidelines (Boundary Sharpening, Cyclic Scheduling, Curriculum Continuity, Local Diversity) and two novel ordering methods (STR and SAW) that reuse pre-computed sample-level scores with minimal overhead, validated across pre-training and SFT stages.
AI.motivation: While data selection for LLM training has been extensively studied, the strategic organization (ordering) of data remains underexplored, especially given that LLMs are typically trained for only one or a few epochs, making order crucial for learning efficiency.
AI.method: The authors formalize four guidelines for data organization and propose two novel ordering methods (STR and SAW) that leverage pre-computed sample-level scores (originally for data efficiency) to reorganize training data with minimal additional computation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across different model scales and data sizes in both pre-training and SFT stages demonstrate the effectiveness of the four guidelines and the robustness of STR and SAW methods in enhancing training stability and performance.
AI.conclusion: Data organization significantly impacts LLM training effectiveness; the proposed guidelines and ordering methods provide a lightweight yet effective approach to improving training outcomes without substantial computational overhead.

title: Locally Coherent, Globally Incoherent: Bounding Compositional Incoherence in Multi-Component LLM Agents
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 24 tables. Preliminary versions to appear at the ICML 2026 Workshops on Combining Theory and Benchmarks (CTB), Statistical Frameworks for Uncertainty in Agentic Systems (AgenticUQ), and Failure Modes of Agentic AI (FAGEN)
summary: Multi-component LLM agents assemble probabilistic claims from components that each see only part of a joint problem; the composition can violate basic probability axioms even when every component is locally coherent. We formalise this locally coherent, globally incoherent failure via the compositional residual eps*, the L2 distance from the composed quote to the joint coherent polytope, computable at runtime from system output and the declared cross-component coupling constraints. A product-structure dichotomy characterises when local coherence suffices, and a Rayleigh-quotient prediction matches the observed residual within 7% on three of four relation classes. A hierarchical Boyle-Dykstra projection repairs the composition deterministically; an anytime-valid e-process gives sequential coherence monitoring. Across 1,876 ensemble cliques on a four-LLM mid-tier panel (frontier-panel rerun in Section 5.5), eps* > 0 on 33-94% of cliques, translating to +0.115 nats per bet of regret on 1,770 resolved bets under the proportional allocation rule (the gain collapses to +0.006 under bettors that themselves coherentise). Three intuitive LLM-side mitigations(retrieval, partition-aware prompting, aggregator-LLM) each fail or regress.

AI.tldr: Multi-component LLM agents produce globally incoherent probability estimates despite local coherence. The paper formalizes this as compositional residual ε*, proposes a Rayleigh-quotient predictor, a hierarchical projection repair, and an anytime-valid e-process for monitoring. Empirically, ε* > 0 on 33-94% of cliques across 1,876 ensemble cliques, causing +0.115 nats regret per bet, and three LLM-side mitigations fail.
AI.motivation: Multi-component LLM agents are increasingly used for probabilistic reasoning, but when each component only sees part of a joint problem, the composed output can violate basic probability axioms even if each component is locally coherent. This gap between local and global coherence is underexplored and can lead to systematic reasoning failures.
AI.method: Formalizes the compositional residual ε* (L2 distance from composed output to the joint coherent polytope). Derives a product-structure dichotomy characterizing when local coherence suffices. Uses Rayleigh-quotient to predict residual magnitude. Develops hierarchical Boyle-Dykstra projection for deterministic repair and an anytime-valid e-process for sequential coherence monitoring. Tests on 1,876 ensemble cliques with four LLMs and 1,770 resolved bets under proportional allocation.
AI.result: ε* > 0 on 33-94% of cliques across 1,876 ensemble cliques. Rayleigh-quotient prediction matches observed residual within 7% on three of four relation classes. Incoherence translates to +0.115 nats per bet regret; collapses to +0.006 when bettors themselves coherentise. Three LLM-side mitigations (retrieval, partition-aware prompting, aggregator-LLM) all fail or cause regression.
AI.conclusion: Local coherence does not guarantee global coherence in multi-component LLM agents; the gap is measurable, predictable, and consequential. Deterministic projection repair and sequential monitoring via e-processes are viable, while naive LLM-side mitigations are ineffective. Systematic coherence auditing is necessary for reliable multi-LLM probabilistic reasoning.

title: Tiny but Trusted: Efficient Vision-Language Reasoning for Time-Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved impressive performance across many tasks, yet prior studies report unsatisfactory performance when applying large language or multimodal models to finding abnormal patterns in sequential data. Public anomaly detection benchmarks typically provide interval annotations but not natural-language rationales, making it difficult to fine-tune VLMs to produce grounded, interpretable decisions. To address this gap, we construct VisAnomBench, a curated benchmark built from public time-series datasets and augmented with high-quality anomaly explanations selected from multiple large VLMs using fine-grained, task-specific rewards. Through fine-tuning on this benchmark, we develop VisAnomReasoner, a parameter-efficient VLM for time-series anomaly detection. Experimental results on VisAnomBench show that VisAnomReasoner achieves more accurate anomaly localization and consistently outperforms all baselines, with improvements of at least 21.23 and 23.87 percentage points in precision and F1, respectively. Additional experiments on the TSB-AD-U benchmark demonstrate strong cross-benchmark generalization, with VisAnomReasoner improving precision and F1 by 9.57 and 13.39 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: VisAnomReasoner is a VLM fine-tuned on VisAnomBench (a curated benchmark with synthetic anomaly explanations) for time-series anomaly detection, outperforming baselines by 21.23+ pp in precision and 23.87+ pp in F1, with strong cross-benchmark generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs perform poorly on anomaly detection in sequential data due to lack of natural-language rationales in public benchmarks, hindering fine-tuning for interpretable decisions.
AI.method: Constructed VisAnomBench from public time-series datasets with high-quality anomaly explanations selected from multiple large VLMs via fine-grained task-specific rewards; then fine-tuned a parameter-efficient VLM (VisAnomReasoner) on this benchmark.
AI.result: VisAnomReasoner achieves at least 21.23 pp higher precision and 23.87 pp higher F1 on VisAnomBench; cross-benchmark (TSB-AD-U) shows +9.57 pp precision and +13.39 pp F1 improvements.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning VLMs with high-quality, reward-selected natural-language explanations significantly improves time-series anomaly detection accuracy and generalization.

title: SchGen: PCB Schematic Generation with Semantic-Grounded Code Representations
summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) schematic design defines nearly all electronic hardware, but it remains manual and expertise-intensive. While generative AI has advanced digital and analog IC design, PCB schematic generation from natural-language intent is largely unexplored. This paper presents SchGen, the first large language model that generates editable PCB schematics from natural-language requests. The key challenge lies in the lack of an LLM-suited representation and a large-scale dataset. Current schematic formats are dominated by verbose, tool-specific syntax and geometry-heavy descriptions, making them difficult to generate reliably. We introduce a semantically grounded code representation that encodes schematic editing primitives with relative placement and pin-name-based wiring, transforming a geometry-driven generation problem into a semantics-driven matching task amenable to LLMs. We further construct a large-scale dataset of PCB schematics paired with user prompts via a human-agent collaborative pipeline that converts open-source hardware designs into our representation. Experiments show that SchGen significantly outperforms alternative representations and even larger general-purpose LLMs on wire connectivity accuracy and functional correctness. Our results highlight the critical role of representation design in enabling generative models for complex hardware design tasks.

AI.tldr: SchGen is the first LLM that generates editable PCB schematics from natural-language requests, using a semantically grounded code representation and a large-scale dataset built via a human-agent pipeline, significantly outperforming baselines on wire connectivity and functional correctness.
AI.motivation: PCB schematic design remains manual and expertise-intensive despite advances in generative AI for IC design; generating PCB schematics from natural-language intent is largely unexplored due to the lack of LLM-suited representations and large-scale datasets.
AI.method: A semantically grounded code representation that encodes schematic editing primitives with relative placement and pin-name-based wiring, transforming geometry-driven generation into a semantics-driven matching task. A large-scale dataset is constructed via a human-agent collaborative pipeline converting open-source hardware designs into this representation.
AI.result: SchGen significantly outperforms alternative representations and even larger general-purpose LLMs on wire connectivity accuracy and functional correctness for PCB schematic generation.
AI.conclusion: Representation design is critical for enabling generative models in complex hardware design tasks; the semantics-driven approach enables reliable PCB schematic generation from natural language.

title: Physics Is All You Need? A Case Study in Physicist-Supervised AI Development of Scientific Software
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, 1 physicist and a few AI agents. Accepted by ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop. Code and development log are available at this repo: https://github.com/MinhMPA/clax-pt
summary:
Are AI agents tools, co-authors, or researchers? We present a quantified case study ($N=1$): a physicist supervising an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Sonnet and Opus models) over 12 work days and 57 sessions to build CLAX-PT, a differentiable one-loop perturbation theory module in JAX. We documented and classified 15 supervision events by intervention level.
  The agent resolved ten autonomously by iterating against oracle tests. Two more by the physicist's domain knowledge. The three it could not -- all evaded oracle detection -- share a common property: the agent treated symptom reduction as root-cause resolution. It spent 33 of the 57 sessions adjusting coefficients within a code architecture that could not represent the target physics, and could not re-evaluate its CLASS-PT branch choice even when prompted to reconsider; only an injected physics concept (anisotropic BAO damping) triggered the redesign. Separately, the agent committed a calibrated correction that passed all oracle tests but corresponded to no quantity in the theory, predicting wrong values at any other cosmology.
  The fudge factor was caught and replaced within the same session. Three supervision practices proved critical for catching what oracle tests missed: testing at diverse parameter points beyond the fiducial calibration; shared changelogs that surfaced stalled exploration across sessions; and an explicit rule against unphysical numerical patches. In this case, supervision design, not model capability, determined whether the agent's output was trustworthy. Closing the gap would require agents that propose architectural alternatives rather than optimize within a given structure, and distinguish predictive adequacy from explanatory correctness -- capabilities not exhibited here, not obviously addressed by scaling alone. [Abridged.]

AI.tldr: A 12-day case study of a physicist supervising an AI coding agent (Claude Code) to build a physics module found that supervision design—not model capability—determined trustworthiness. The agent repeatedly failed by treating symptom reduction as root-cause resolution, and three critical practices (diverse parameter testing, shared changelogs, and anti-patching rules) were essential for catching errors that oracle tests missed.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether AI agents can function as reliable research tools in scientific computation, specifically quantifying failure modes and supervision practices needed to ensure trustworthy outputs beyond what standard testing (oracle tests) can catch.
AI.method: A quantified N=1 case study: a physicist supervised Claude Code (Sonnet and Opus models) over 12 work days and 57 sessions to build CLAX-PT, a differentiable one-loop perturbation theory module in JAX. 15 supervision events were documented and classified by intervention level, with analysis of which the agent could resolve autonomously, which required human domain knowledge, and which it could not resolve.
AI.result: The agent autonomously resolved 10/15 issues by iterating against oracle tests. Two more required the physicist's domain knowledge. Three could not be resolved—all shared the property of treating symptom reduction as root-cause resolution, spending 33/57 sessions adjusting coefficients within an architecture incapable of representing the target physics. The agent also committed a calibrated "fudge factor" that passed all oracle tests but predicted wrong values at other cosmologies.
AI.conclusion: Supervision design, not model capability, determined trustworthiness. Closing the gap requires agents that propose architectural alternatives rather than optimize within fixed structures, and distinguish predictive adequacy from explanatory correctness—capabilities not obviously solved by scaling alone.
